chats.title: At-risk authorisation — black lambskin leather jacket, docket K-09104

messages.content: I've got a customer at the counter, Sione Latu, black AllSaints lambskin biker, and I've stopped short of booking it in. The right sleeve is two shades lighter than the rest where he drives with his arm out the window, the finish is worn right through at both cuffs and along the collar, and there's a stiff patch about 150 across on the lower back where something's dried into it. He wants it cleaned and that back mark out. Label says leather specialist only, colour change may occur. It's a 2021 jacket, he says $1,100. Karen's seen my photos and says take it but only on an at-risk. What do I put on it?

Take it, but only on a signed authorisation, and the authorisation has to be signed before it leaves your counter — not posted afterwards.

The reasoning is that everything wrong with this jacket now will be worse or different after cleaning, and none of it will be our doing. Leather is a skin, not a woven fabric. Its colour is an applied surface finish over a substrate that varies in density and oil content across a single hide, and cleaning necessarily takes some of that finish and some of the natural oils along with the soil. Where the finish is already worn through — both cuffs, the collar fold — it will go further. DLI TABS — Leather, Suede, Velvet & Napped Fabrics records colour change, further finish loss on worn areas and the permanence of set stains as inherent outcomes rather than cleaner error, and it flags a garment that is already uneven before cleaning as materially higher risk. This one is halfway there before we start.

Method: send it out to the specialist, and re-finish the whole jacket rather than spot-finish it. Spot re-finishing the cuffs and collar on a jacket whose sleeve is already two shades out will show every edge. Tell him 3 to 4 weeks, not our usual 5 days.

The risks he has to sign to are: the colour will change and may not come back to the original black; further finish loss at the cuffs and collar is likely; the back mark may not lift at all and the stiffening may stay even if the colour is covered; and the quilted shoulder panels are a textile, not leather, so they may not take the re-finish evenly.

Your nine photographs are the other half of the file. Keep them against the docket.

I'd draw this up as a printed at-risk authorisation for him to sign at the counter — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: At-risk authorisation — black lambskin leather jacket, docket K-09104

chats.title: Navy down puffer jacket — docket B-25491

messages.content: Fiona Brereton brought her navy Kathmandu puffer back in on Saturday, docket B-25491, we did it on the 20th. She says it's flat and lumpy and she's getting cold spots along the top. Emma had a look and agreed the down's all clumped at the bottom of each baffle. We wet cleaned it on the down programme like the label says and gave it one tumble with the balls after, which is what we normally do. Emma offered to take it back and run a longer re-loft free but she's gone off saying she wants it back how it was or the price of a new one. It's a $520 jacket. What do I do?

This is not a claim, and I would be careful not to let it turn into one by treating it like one.

Nothing is damaged. Down is loose cluster, not batting, and it moves inside the baffle. Washing wets the clusters, they collapse together, and as the jacket dries they settle to the bottom of each channel and clump, which thins the top of every baffle and gives you exactly the cold spots she is describing. The shell, the baffle stitching, the lining and the down are all sound. It is a drying-stage outcome, and it reverses.

DLI TABS — Household Textiles, covering drapes, comforters, down and linens, records clumping after cleaning as expected rather than exceptional, and recovered by extended low-heat tumbling that separates the clusters and returns the loft. Fill power is not lost. The down just needs to be beaten apart again.

Where we did fall short is the drying, and it is fair to say so without turning it into fault. One low-heat tumble with dryer balls is our standard and it suits most jackets. A hip-length hooded jacket with horizontal baffles and 700 fill duck down is a lot of down in deep channels, and one cycle has not done it. Two or three will, with the clumps hand-broken between cycles.

So: no settlement figure, no admission, and do not put a number on the jacket — the moment you value it you have conceded it is a claim. Offer the extended re-loft at no charge, put a $40 credit on her account for having to come back twice, and make it easy — Sharon expecting her at the counter, or Dylan collects.

Keep it short and warm. She has gone away annoyed and the letter's job is to get the jacket back in the door.

I'd put that offer in a short goodwill letter to Fiona — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Navy down puffer jacket — docket B-25491

chats.title: What does the lease actually say about the rent review?

messages.content: Castleton have sent through a notice saying the rent goes up in March. I want to know what the lease actually allows them to do before I ring them back, because last year they came in higher than I expected and I did not have the document in front of me. What is the review mechanism and is there anything I should be checking?

Your lease reviews the rent to CPI on 1 March each year — Melbourne All Groups — and there is no market review and no ratchet in the mechanism itself. So the number is arithmetic, not negotiation, and it should be checkable in about two minutes.

Base rent is $58,400 plus GST, which is $4,866.67 a month. Applied to the CPI movement for the relevant period, that gives you a figure you can compute yourself rather than accept. Ask Castleton to state which index period they have used. That is the single most common place these go wrong — using a quarter that has not been published yet, or using the Australia-wide figure rather than Melbourne.

Two other things worth checking while you have it open. Your outgoings are estimated at $9,200 a year and the Retail Leases Act obliges the landlord to give you a written estimate before each year and then reconcile it against what was actually spent. If you have not had a reconciliation for the last year, ask for it — you are entitled to it and it is sometimes in your favour.

And the Act prohibits a landlord recovering land tax from a retail tenant in Victoria. It is worth reading down the outgoings line by line for anything that looks like it, because it does turn up.

On timing: your first five-year term runs to 28 February 2029, and the option to renew has an exercise window that you do not want to discover late. That is a 2028 problem, but it is the kind that is expensive if it is missed.

Do you want me to draft the reply to Castleton asking them to substantiate the index period and provide the outgoings reconciliation?

letterOffer.subject: Rent review — request to substantiate the CPI calculation and provide the outgoings reconciliation

chats.title: Boiler keeps dropping out on B05

messages.content: Peter rang me at ten past seven — the Fulton has dropped out and the panel is showing B05. He has hit reset twice and it goes again after about a minute. We have got yesterday's racks still to press and no steam. Is this something he can sort out or do I need to get someone in?

B05 on the FB-030 is LOW WATER — FIRST: the level has fallen to the first low water tip and the burner is being held off. That is the control doing exactly what it is there for.

The important part is the reset class. B05 is Class A once — resettable a single time, and Class B if it comes back. Peter has now reset it twice, and the manual is blunt about why that matters: a single B05 at the start of a heavy Monday with a hotwell nobody refilled over the weekend is explicable. A B05 that recurs is not, because the boiler has six minutes of water at full fire and something is taking it away.

So stop resetting, and work the feedwater side in the order the manual sets out. Is there water in the hotwell. Is the make-up supply on. Is the softener stuck in regeneration and starving the hotwell. Is the feed pump running when it is called. Is the feed line stop valve open. Is the strainer blocked. Is the bottom blowdown valve passing — that shows as a hot blowdown line between blowdowns. Is there a visible leak.

Two things he must not do. Do not add water if the gauge glass is empty. And if it goes to B06 — LOW WATER, SECOND, LOCKOUT — that is the first device having failed to protect, and it is stop, do not reset, do not add water, isolate the gas, call the technician. B06 is Class B and an operator may never clear it.

Given it has already come back twice, my call is to get your boiler technician out this morning rather than lose the day. Goldfields did your June inspection so they know the machine — and worth knowing, that report already flagged your daily logs had three gaps in May, which is the kind of thing that gets asked about if this turns into something.

Want me to draft the service request?

letterOffer.subject: Service request — Fulton FB-030, recurring B05 low water

chats.title: Ivory silk wedding gown, clean and preserve — docket B-22140

messages.content: Alana Petrides came in Monday with her wedding gown box, docket B-22140. We cleaned and boxed it in February after her January wedding, ivory silk mikado, and she opened it on Saturday to show her sister. There's a broad yellow-brown discolouration across the bodice and down the right side of the skirt, worst on the fold lines. Karen opened the box with her here. The tissue in it is ordinary white tissue, not the acid-free we sell the preserve service on, and it's one of the old boxes. We've kept the tissue and photographed the lot. The invoice from Rosalind Bridal is $3,200 and that's what she wants.

This is ours and there is no way out of it worth looking for. We sell the preserve service on acid-free materials and this box was not packed with them.

The mechanism is acid migration. Ordinary tissue is manufactured with residual acidity and releases acidic gases as it ages, and in a closed box against silk over six months that produces yellow-brown discolouration that follows the fold lines — worst where the fabric is folded hardest, which matches the bodice and the right skirt panel exactly. DLI TABS — Colour Fading & Discoloration treats it as a storage fault rather than a cleaning fault, and the clean itself is not in question: programme 8 on the Realstar, cleaned alone, hem mark reduced by hand and the residual recorded on the docket and shown to her at collection.

On the number there are two steps and she needs to see both. The Guide gives a post-wedding gown a three year life. At 10 months she is in the 10 to 19 month band, condition excellent, which adjusts to 70 per cent — $2,240 on a $3,200 invoice. But the Guide then caps a gown after the wedding at 50 per cent of replacement cost, because it has already served its purpose and is not in ongoing use. Half of $3,200 is $1,600, so the adjustment drops to the cap. The offer is $1,600.00 and the $295.00 clean and preserve charge is refunded.

Explain that cap in terms. A customer who is only told "70 per cent, then $1,600" will assume they are being short-changed.

One more thing worth offering: attempt a staged reduction of the discolouration at our cost. Result not guaranteed, but she may want the gown more than the money, and it costs us a spotting board and a day.

I'd set the working, the cap and that offer out in a settlement letter to Alana — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Ivory silk wedding gown, clean and preserve — docket B-22140

messages.content: Geoffrey Wan's camel cashmere jumper, docket B-25277, Country Road, came in for wet clean on the strength of the label — hand wash 30, dry flat, and it's got the W as well. We've done it twice before with no trouble. Marco pulled it out of Speed Queen 2 on Monday and it's felted right through, chest is 430 flat where it was 560 at intake, body's 70 shorter, ribbing's gone tight. Peter checked the log and the wool cycle was set to 40 with a general extract instead of 30 and reduced. It's been fixed and locked since. He paid $640 in June last year and wants it replaced.

We pay this, and we tell him exactly why. A misconfigured programme in our own log is not something to be vague about.

The cause is settled by the log. Cashmere felts when heat, moisture and mechanical action let the scale structure on the fibre interlock, and it is irreversible once it happens — the fibres are physically hooked together, not merely compressed. Ten degrees and a general extract instead of a reduced one is precisely the margin between a safe wool cycle and a felted one. DLI TABS — Stretch, Shrinkage & Distortion covers the mechanism and confirms there is no recovery process: blocking a felted knit out to measurement tears it before it moves.

The method choice was right, which is worth saying to him. The label authorised professional wet cleaning and we had wet cleaned the same jumper in September 2025 and again in March 2026 without a mark on it. The failure was the machine parameter, not the decision. Say that the machine has been re-parameterised and the wool settings locked at the panel — a customer who hears that a fault was found and closed usually stops looking for an argument.

On the number, the Fair Claims Guide gives a wool jumper or cardigan a four year life. At 14 months it falls in the 13 to 25 month band, condition excellent — well kept, two prior cleans without incident, only the small moth repair Anh did at the left underarm in March. That band adjusts to 70 per cent, so on $640 the offer is $448.00, and waive the $24.00 charge.

That percentage is high because the garment was young, and it is worth showing him the working so it reads as a standard rather than a guess. Offer the jumper back as well; some people want the garment regardless.

I'd write that up as a settlement letter to Geoffrey — want me to draft it?

chats.title: Emerald silk wrap dress — docket K-08812

messages.content: This is a bad one and it's mine. Priya Raman dropped an emerald Scanlan Theodore silk wrap dress here at the Flat on the 13th, docket K-08812. It's got a matching self belt and I left it threaded through the loops, so it went to Bendigo and through the machine with the dress. The belt's a different dye lot, always been a deeper green. Dye has bled into both hips and the small of the back, three patches with soft edges. Peter got maybe a third of it out on the board and Karen stopped him. Label actually says remove belt before cleaning. She's worn it twice and wants $680. I'm sorry.

We pay this one. There is no defensible version and it is better to say so quickly than slowly.

The care label carried a specific instruction — remove belt before cleaning — and our own intake procedure says belts, sashes, scarves and detachable trims come off at the counter and get bagged separately. Two independent instructions, both missed. That is preparation, not process: programme 5 on the Union was the right cycle for a silk crepe de chine and the dress would have come out perfectly if the belt had been in a separate bag.

A separate dye lot on the belt is the aggravating fact. Emerald acid dyes on silk are among the worst for migration, and lot-to-lot variation in fixation is exactly the case where one piece bleeds onto another in solvent. DLI TABS — Dye Bleed, Migration & Colour Run covers it, and it is also why Karen was right to stop Peter. Once a bled dye has set into a silk ground, further reduction takes the ground colour before it takes the stain, and three patches become a ruined dress.

On the number, the Fair Claims Guide classes it as a fancy dress with a two year life. At eight months it sits in the 7 to 13 month band, condition excellent — worn twice, first clean. That band adjusts to 70 per cent, so on $680 the offer is $476.00, and waive the $28.00 charge.

Do not hedge the cause when you write to her. She knows what happened, we know what happened, and a customer who is told plainly that we made an error usually takes the depreciated figure without a fight. Offer to return the dress too — the marks sit where a jacket would cover them.

I'd put that in a settlement letter to Priya, cause stated plainly and the working shown — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Emerald silk wrap dress — docket K-08812

chats.title: Navy beaded evening gown — docket B-24118

messages.content: Need a hand with this one. Marguerite Oakley, docket B-24118, navy Carla Zampatti beaded gown, all-over bugle beading. I booked it in on the 10th, flagged the beads as plastic not glass and told her they might not survive solvent, and she signed the at-risk form. Peter ran it in the Realstar on programme 6, the beaded one, so hydrocarbon not perc even though the label says P. Out of the machine about 15 per cent of the beads on the bodice have gone cloudy and matt. No beads off, fabric is perfect. She wants $890, what she paid at Myer in 2023. Where do we actually stand?

We defend this one, and we defend it confidently.

Three things decide it. The label permits reduced perc and you used hydrocarbon on programme 6 — a four minute bath, no spin above 200 rpm, 38 degrees with an extended cool-down. That is materially gentler than the process the manufacturer authorised, and a cleaner who goes gentler than the label cannot be said to have exceeded it. Second, the damage is confined to one component. The polyester ground is unmarked, unshrunk and unringed and the stitching is intact. A cleaning fault shows in the ground fabric first, every time. When only the beads have changed, the beads are the problem. Third, you have the signed at-risk authorisation from 10 June naming the beading and the possibility of clouding, plus six intake photographs and four after.

The technical basis is DLI TABS — Prints, Embellishments, Trims & Notions. It records that coated and surface-finished beads can dull, craze or delaminate in any professional solvent depending on the coating chemistry the trim supplier chose, and that this cannot be predicted or prevented by a cleaner following the care label. There is no counter test for a bead coating. The International Fair Claims Guide puts responsibility for a component that fails in a label-permitted process with whoever specified the component — the manufacturer.

Worth adding: the label says nothing about the beading at all. AS/NZS 1957 requires care instructions to account for trim, so the labelling is non-compliant, and that is the manufacturer's problem too.

Next step: send her back to Myer Bendigo with something in writing she can hand across the counter. I would also offer to have Anh re-bead the bodice at our cost, so she has a way to keep the gown rather than a fight.

I'd put the technical position in a To Whom It May Concern letter she can take to Myer — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Navy beaded evening gown — docket B-24118

chats.title: Charcoal wool suit jacket — docket B-23904

messages.content: Trevor Lindsay just came back in with the jacket off his charcoal Hugo Boss, docket B-23904, cleaned 22 May. The collar and both shoulders have gone about two shades lighter than the rest and there's a tide line where the collar meets the body. Trousers went through the same load and they're fine. Karen's looked at it in daylight and agrees. Perc, Union, programme 3, standard tailored cycle — no pre-spot on the collar and nothing about build-up written on the docket. Chloe booked it in. He paid $1,250 for the suit in 2023 and he wants it replaced. What am I telling him?

This one is ours, at least in part, and I would settle it rather than argue it.

The mechanism is straightforward. Hair product, skin oil and perspiration concentrate on the collar and the shoulder tops and weaken the dye in situ over time. The next perc cycle lifts the weakened dye along with the soil, and you get local colour loss with a hard edge at the collar seam. The trousers being untouched confirms the machine was behaving — it is the soil pattern, not the cycle. DLI TABS — Colour Fading & Discoloration sets out that mechanism and the correct handling, which is to identify the affected areas at intake and pre-spot or divert.

That is where we are exposed. Our own SOP says a collar showing product build-up goes to hydrocarbon or gets pre-spotted. Neither happened, nothing was noted at intake, and there are no intake photographs. We could talk about contributory factors all day but a Consumer Affairs officer would read our procedure, see we did not follow it, and stop there.

On the number, the Fair Claims Guide gives a wool suit a three year life. His is 36 months old, which is the 28 to 37 month band, condition average — sound and well kept but at the end of the expected life. That band adjusts to 20 per cent, so on $1,250 the offer is $250.00, and I would waive the $32.00 cleaning charge.

He will think $250 is low against a $1,250 suit, so the working has to be visible and the tone has to be straight. Do not hedge it, do not lead with sympathy, and do not tell him the collar was already weak — say we should have caught it and did not. Offer to return the suit if he would rather keep the trousers.

I'd set all of that out in a settlement letter to him — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Charcoal wool suit jacket — docket B-23904

chats.title: Four pairs lined curtains — docket B-22886

messages.content: Deborah Kastellorizos rang Thursday about her four pairs of pinch pleats, docket B-22886. In on the 30th, cleaned on the 2nd, collected on the 4th. She says two pairs no longer reach the floor and the hems are pulling. I measured 2,650 at intake and it's on the docket; Karen went out to the house Tuesday and they're hanging at 2,610. Cotton linen union with a cotton lining, made in 2019, never cleaned in seven years, no pre-shrink per her maker's invoice. No care label on them at all. She signed the drapery advice on the 30th. She wants $2,400 for new ones. Can we hold the line?

We hold the line on liability, but we do not leave her with short curtains.

The measurements do the work. 2,650 mm at intake, 2,610 mm hung, so 40 mm on a 2,650 mm drop is 1.5 per cent. Relaxation shrinkage of up to 3 per cent is accepted across the trade as normal in drapery, so she is at half the allowance. Every fact points the same way: a cotton and linen union face over a cotton sateen lining, two natural fibres with different shrinkage behaviour, no pre-shrink treatment from the maker, and seven years hanging under its own weight without ever being cleaned. Curtains stretch on the rail and hold the stretch. The first clean releases it. That is the fabric's history, not our machine, and programme 9 is the mildest cycle we run on a lined curtain — 180 rpm, hung to relax straight out of the drum.

DLI TABS — Stretch, Shrinkage & Distortion states it as an inherent fabric characteristic that is neither caused nor preventable by the cleaning process. Note too that there is no care label on these at all, so there was no manufacturer's instruction as to process or shrinkage allowance and we worked to our own judgement at the mildest setting available.

The signed drapery advice from 30 March is what makes this a short conversation rather than a long one. It says in terms that up to 3 per cent relaxation is normal and not a fault. That is why we measure at the counter.

So: deny liability, decline the $2,400, and then fix her problem. There is turn-up in those hems and 40 mm is well inside it. Anh lets all four pairs down and re-presses at our cost, no charge, and Dylan can collect if she would rather not carry them in.

I'd put the denial and the free alteration in one letter to her — want me to draft it?

letterOffer.subject: Four pairs lined curtains — docket B-22886

letters.subject: Navy down puffer jacket — docket B-25491
letters.body:
Dear Fiona,

Thank you for bringing the jacket back in on Saturday and for giving us the chance to look at it rather than just leaving it in the cupboard. Emma and I have both had a good look and I want to tell you what is going on, because it is better news than it looks.

The down has not been damaged. What has happened is that it has migrated. Down is loose clusters, not batting, and it moves freely inside each baffle. Washing wets those clusters, they collapse against each other, and as the jacket dries they clump and settle to the bottom of each channel. That leaves the top of every baffle thin, which is why the jacket feels flat and lumpy and why you are getting cold spots along the shoulders and the upper chest. The shell, the baffle stitching, the lining and the down itself are all sound. Nothing in your jacket is broken.

It is also a completely normal outcome and a recoverable one. DLI TABS — Household Textiles, which covers drapes, comforters, down and linens, records that clumping of down after cleaning is expected rather than exceptional, and that it is recovered by extended low-heat tumbling which separates the clusters and returns the loft. The down does not lose its fill power; it just needs to be beaten apart again.

Where we fell short is on the drying. Our standard is one low-heat tumble with dryer balls after the wash, and for most jackets that is enough. Yours is a hip-length hooded jacket with horizontal baffles and 700 fill power duck down, which is a lot of down in deep channels, and one cycle has not done the job. It needs two or three.

So here is what we would like to do. Bring the jacket back in and we will run a full extended re-loft at no charge — usually two to three cycles on low heat with dryer balls, checking and hand-breaking the clumps between cycles, which takes most of a day. In our experience that brings a jacket like yours back to where it was. We are also putting a $40 credit on your account for the trouble of having to come back in twice.

Just drop it at the Hargreaves Street counter whenever it suits you. Sharon knows to expect you, so you will not have to explain any of it again. If you would rather not make the trip, ring us on (03) 5443 8817 and Dylan will pick it up on his next run. Either way we will have it back to you within two working days.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: At-risk authorisation — black lambskin leather jacket, docket K-09104
letters.body:
AUTHORISATION TO PROCEED — GARMENT ACCEPTED AT CUSTOMER'S RISK

Customer: Sione Latu
Telephone: 0466 812 340
Docket number: K-09104
Site: Kangaroo Flat drop store, Shop 12, Lansell Square, 233 High Street, Kangaroo Flat VIC 3555
Date: 24/08/2026
Staff member: Rebecca Toomey

THE GARMENT

AllSaints black lambskin biker jacket, asymmetric front zip, quilted polyester shoulder panels, viscose lining. Purchased from AllSaints Melbourne in 2021; approximately 5 years old. Value stated by the customer: $1,100. Service requested by the customer: full clean and removal of the mark on the lower back.

THE CARE LABEL

Present and legible, stitched into the lining seam. It carries no care symbol. The tag reads, in full: "By leather specialist only — colour change may occur."

CONDITION AT INTAKE

The following were present when the jacket was handed over the counter and were photographed before it was accepted. Nine photographs were taken, including the sleeve colour difference, both cuffs, the collar and the back mark with a scale.

1. The right sleeve is approximately two shades lighter than the body and the left sleeve. This is sun bleaching, consistent with the customer's account of driving with that arm at the window.
2. The applied surface finish is worn through to the bare skin at both cuffs, on the outer face, over an area of roughly 60 mm on each.
3. The applied surface finish is worn through along the full length of the collar fold.
4. Colour is uneven across the front and back panels generally, independent of the sleeve difference.
5. A stiffened area approximately 150 mm across sits on the lower back, where a liquid of unknown composition has dried into the skin. The hand of the leather in that area is noticeably harder than the surrounding panels.
6. The quilted polyester shoulder panels are a different substrate to the leather and have worn and soiled differently.
7. General wear consistent with five years of use: creasing at the elbows, softening at the front edges, minor scuffing at the hem.

WHAT WE PROPOSE TO DO

The jacket will not be cleaned in our own plant. It will be sent to our specialist leather cleaner, who will clean it in a leather-specific process and then re-finish it. The whole jacket will be re-finished, not spot-finished. Spot re-finishing the cuffs, collar and back would leave visible edges where new finish meets old, and on a jacket whose colour is already uneven it would look worse than what you have now. Re-finishing the whole garment is the only way to bring the panels back to one colour.

THE RISKS

1. The colour will change. Re-finishing lays down new colour over the whole jacket and it may not return to the original shade. The finished jacket may read lighter, darker or slightly different in tone to the black you brought in.
2. Further loss of finish at the cuffs and along the collar fold is likely. Cleaning removes soil and it also removes finish that is already failing. Those areas may look worse before they are re-finished, and the new finish may not hold as well there as it does elsewhere.
3. The mark on the lower back may not come out at all. It is set, it has stiffened the skin, and its composition is unknown. The stiffening may remain even if the colour of the mark is covered by the re-finish.
4. The quilted shoulder panels may not take the re-finish evenly. They are a textile, not leather, and they will absorb finish differently to the skin around them.
5. Turnaround is 3 to 4 weeks, not our usual 5 days, because the work is done off site.

THE DLI POSITION

DLI TABS — Leather, Suede, Velvet & Napped Fabrics records that these risks are inherent to leather cleaning rather than the result of any error by the cleaner. Leather is a natural skin, not a woven fabric. Its colour is an applied surface finish over a substrate that varies in density, oil content and absorbency across a single hide, and cleaning necessarily removes some of the natural oils and some of that finish along with the soil. The TAB records that colour change, further loss of finish on already worn areas, and the permanence of set stains are expected outcomes on a worn garment, and that a garment already showing uneven colour and worn finish before cleaning carries a materially higher risk of an uneven result. That description fits this jacket.

AUTHORISATION

I have read the condition report and the risks set out above and I have had them explained to me. I understand that this jacket is accepted at my risk, and that Main Street Dry Cleaners does not accept liability for colour change, further loss of finish, failure of the mark on the lower back to lift, or uneven finish on the quilted panels. I authorise Main Street Dry Cleaners to send the jacket to its specialist leather cleaner and to have it cleaned and fully re-finished on that basis.

I understand that this authorisation does not exclude, restrict or modify the consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law that cannot be excluded. Our services must still be supplied with due care and skill, and nothing signed here changes that or removes any right I have if they are not.

Customer signature: ......................................................

Printed name: Sione Latu

Date: ......../......../2026

Staff signature: ......................................................

Printed name: Rebecca Toomey

Date: ......../......../2026

letters.subject: Ivory silk wedding gown, clean and preserve — docket B-22140
letters.body:
Dear Alana,

The discolouration you found when you opened the box on 8 August was caused by the way we packed your gown, and we accept responsibility for it. You paid us for a clean and preserve service and the preserving half of it was not done properly.

The clean itself was sound. The gown was cleaned on 11 February in hydrocarbon on our bridal programme, alone, with the hem mark reduced by hand on the spotting board, and the residual hem mark was recorded on the docket and shown to you when you collected. It went into the box in good order. What went wrong was the packing on 13 February. Our preserve service is sold on acid-free, unbuffered tissue and an archival box, and this gown was interleaved with ordinary white tissue from older stock. Ordinary tissue is made with residual acidity and it releases acidic gases as it ages in a closed box. Over six months against silk, that produces exactly what you have — a broad yellow-brown discolouration following the fold lines, worst on the bodice and down the right skirt panel where the fabric was folded hardest. We have kept the tissue and photographed it with the box and the gown together. DLI TABS — Colour Fading & Discoloration describes this as acid migration from non-archival packaging, and it is a storage fault, not a cleaning fault. It is ours either way.

On the money. Textile claims are settled on the International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products, which is the standard the trade, the insurers and Consumer Affairs all work from, and it settles on depreciated value rather than the price of a new one. The Guide gives a wedding gown after the wedding a normal life expectancy of three years. Yours is 10 months old, which puts it in the 10 to 19 month band, and its condition is excellent. That band at excellent condition adjusts to 70 per cent, which on the $3,200 invoiced by Rosalind Bridal would be $2,240.

There is a second step that applies to wedding gowns specifically, and I want to set it out rather than have the number appear from nowhere. The Guide caps a gown after the wedding at 50 per cent of its replacement cost, on the basis that a wedding gown has already served the purpose it was bought for and is not a garment in ongoing use. Half of $3,200 is $1,600, so the 70 per cent adjustment is reduced to the cap. Our offer is $1,600.00. The clean and preserve charge of $295.00 is waived and will be refunded to you in full.

There is something else worth considering before you decide. You may want the gown more than the money. We are willing to attempt a reduction of the discolouration at our own cost — a controlled bleaching and rinse sequence on silk mikado, done in stages with a stop at each one. I will not promise a result. Acid discolouration of this age sometimes comes back a long way and sometimes barely moves, and there is a real risk of losing evenness across the panels. But it costs you nothing to let us try, and if it works you keep your gown. If you would like us to attempt it, we will do the work first and settle afterwards, so you can see the result before you decide.

On payment of the full adjusted value the gown becomes our property, which is the ordinary position under the Guide. If you would rather keep it, whether or not we attempt the reduction, tell us and it stays yours.

Ring Sharon or me on (03) 5443 8817, or reply to this letter, and tell us three things: whether you accept the $1,600.00, whether you want us to attempt the reduction first, and whether you want to keep the gown. Payment goes out by electronic transfer within five business days of you confirming, to any account you nominate.

I am sorry. A gown boxed for keeping should have been kept properly, and yours was not.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Camel cashmere jumper — docket B-25277
letters.body:
Dear Geoffrey,

Your cashmere jumper was felted and shrunk in our plant, by our machine, on a programme that was set wrong. That is our fault and we are not going to argue any part of it with you.

The jumper came in on docket B-25277 and was wet cleaned on 3 August. Your care label reads hand wash at 30, do not tumble dry, dry flat, and it also carries the professional wet clean "W", so wet cleaning was the right call — it is what we did with the same jumper in September 2025 and again in March 2026 without a mark on it. What was not right was the machine. When Marco pulled it out felted, Peter went straight to the programme log on Speed Queen washer 2, and the wool cycle was running a 40 degree wash with a general extract, where our wool programme is specified at 30 degrees with a reduced extract. Ten degrees and a hard extract is the whole difference between washing cashmere and felting it. The machine has since been re-parameterised and the wool settings locked so they cannot be altered at the panel.

The damage is not recoverable. The chest measures 430 mm flat against 560 mm at intake and the body has lost 70 mm in length, the surface has felted across the body and sleeves, and the ribbing at the cuffs and hem has tightened and will not relax. DLI TABS — Stretch, Shrinkage & Distortion sets out why: felting in an animal fibre is the mechanical interlocking of the scale structure under heat and agitation, and it is permanent. There is no process that reverses it. Blocking it out would tear the fabric before it moved the measurements.

On the money. Textile claims are settled on the International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products, which is the standard the trade and the insurers work to, and it pays depreciated value rather than the cost of a new one. The Guide gives a wool jumper or cardigan a normal life expectancy of four years. Yours is 14 months old, which sits in the 13 to 25 month band, and its condition is excellent — well kept, cleaned twice by us without incident, with only the small moth repair we did at the left underarm in March. That band at excellent condition adjusts to 70 per cent of replacement cost. On a replacement cost of $640, that is $448.00.

I would rather explain the number than have it look invented. It is not the price of a new jumper, and it is not meant to be. Textile claims are settled on what remains of a garment's useful life, and a fourteen month old jumper has most of that life left, which is why the percentage here is high rather than low.

Our offer is $448.00. The cleaning charge of $24.00 is waived — you will not be billed for it, and if it has already been taken we will refund it with the settlement.

On payment of the full adjusted value the jumper becomes our property, which is the ordinary position under the Guide. If you would rather keep it, say so and we will return it. It will not fit you, but people do want the garment back, and we would rather you had the choice.

Ring Emma or me on (03) 5443 8817, or reply to this letter, and tell us whether you want the jumper back. Payment goes out by electronic transfer within five business days of you confirming, to any account you nominate.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Change of ordinary hours — Julie Harmon, from 5 October 2026
letters.body:
Dear Julie,

This letter confirms what we agreed when we spoke on 5 August 2026 about your hours from the start of Term 4.

You are currently engaged as a permanent part-time shirt presser working 25 hours a week, Monday to Friday, 9:30am to 2:30pm. You have asked to reduce that to four days a week from Monday 5 October 2026 because of the change to your daughter's school days, and to keep the same daily start and finish.

We are happy to agree to it. From 5 October 2026 your ordinary hours will be 20 hours a week, worked Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, 9:30am to 2:30pm. Your classification stays at Dry Cleaning DC2 under the Dry Cleaning and Laundry Industry Award 2020 and your hourly rate is unchanged. Your leave entitlements will accrue on the new hours from that date, and the leave you have already accrued is unaffected.

Two things worth saying out loud. Your Wednesday shirt volume will go to Chloe with Marco covering the overflow, so you are not walking back into a backlog on Thursday mornings. And this is a permanent change to your agreement rather than a temporary arrangement, so if you want to go back to five days later on, that is a conversation and an agreement rather than something that happens automatically. I am not saying that to make it hard — I am saying it so nobody is surprised in March.

If this does not match your understanding of what we agreed, tell me before 5 October and we will sort it out. Otherwise please sign and return the attached copy and we will put it on your file.

Thanks for giving us as much notice as you did. It made it easy to cover.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Offer of casual conversion — Dylan Pearce
letters.body:
Dear Dylan,

You have been working with us as a casual since 2 October 2023. Under the Fair Work Act we are required to look at whether a casual employee has been working a regular pattern of hours that could continue as a permanent employee, and to make an offer where that is the case. We have looked at yours, and it is.

Over the last twelve months you have worked an average of 25.4 hours a week across a settled pattern — Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, starting at 7:30am and finishing between 1:00pm and 2:30pm depending on the run. That pattern has not varied much since the second half of 2024. It is, in substance, a part-time job.

So we are offering to convert your employment to permanent part-time, effective from the first pay period on or after 22 September 2026, on these terms:

Twenty-five ordinary hours a week, worked Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, 7:30am to 1:45pm, at the Dry Cleaning DC2 classification under the Dry Cleaning and Laundry Industry Award 2020. Your ordinary hourly rate will be the DC2 part-time rate, which is lower than what you are paid now, because the 25% casual loading stops. In exchange you would accrue paid annual leave and paid personal/carer's leave, you would be paid on public holidays you would ordinarily have worked, and your employment would carry notice of termination and redundancy entitlements that a casual does not have.

We have set out both the current and proposed rates on the attached sheet so you can see the difference in a normal week and across a year. On our figures you are slightly ahead over twelve months once leave is counted, but I would rather you check that yourself than take my word for it.

You do not have to accept. If you would prefer to stay casual, say so and nothing changes — it will not affect your shifts, your run, or how we treat you, and we will look at it again in twelve months. If you want to talk it through first, or bring someone with you to do that, you are welcome to, and I would encourage it either way.

Please let me know in writing by 15 September 2026 either way.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Emerald silk wrap dress — docket K-08812
letters.body:
Dear Priya,

The dye transfer on your emerald silk dress is our fault. We left the belt threaded through the loops and put it through the machine with the dress, and there is no version of this where that is anything other than our error.

The dress was dropped at our Kangaroo Flat store on 13 July and cleaned at Bendigo on 14 July under docket K-08812. The care label carries a supplementary line reading "Remove belt before cleaning". Our own intake procedure says the same thing in broader terms — belts, sashes, scarves and detachable trims come off at the counter and are bagged separately. The belt is the same silk as the dress but was dyed in a separate lot, which is why it has always been a deeper green, and a separate lot of an emerald acid dye on silk is exactly the case where dye will migrate in solvent. It did. You now have three darker patches with soft edges, at both hips and across the small of the back, between about 60 mm and 110 mm across.

Peter worked on it on the spotting board on 15 July and lifted perhaps a third of it. Karen then stopped him, because the next step risked pulling the ground colour out of the dress around the marks and turning three patches into a much larger problem. DLI TABS — Dye Bleed, Migration & Colour Run is clear that once a bled dye has set into a silk ground, aggressive reduction usually costs more colour than it recovers. So the marks that are there now are the marks that will stay.

On the money. Textile claims are settled on the International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products, which is the standard the industry, insurers and Consumer Affairs work from, and it settles on depreciated value rather than the price of a new one. The Guide classes this as a fancy dress with a normal life expectancy of two years. Yours is eight months old, which falls in the 7 to 13 month band, and its condition is excellent — worn twice, never cleaned before, and sound in every respect apart from what we did to it. That band at excellent condition adjusts to 70 per cent of replacement cost. On a replacement cost of $680, that is $476.00.

That is depreciated value, not a new dress, and I would rather be straight about it than have you find out from someone else. It is how every textile claim in the country is worked out, and it is the number we would be held to by our own insurer.

Our offer is $476.00. The cleaning charge of $28.00 is waived and will not be billed to you; if it has already gone through, we will refund it.

On payment of the full adjusted value the dress becomes our property, which is the ordinary position under the Guide. If you would rather keep it — the marks sit where a jacket or a coat would cover them, and it is otherwise a sound dress — tell us and it is yours to keep.

To accept, ring us on (03) 5443 8817 or reply to this letter and let us know which way you want to go on the dress. We will pay by electronic transfer within five business days of hearing from you, to any account you nominate.

We are sorry. You left us a new dress and a clear instruction, and we did not follow it.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Navy beaded evening gown — docket B-24118
letters.body:
To Whom It May Concern,

We confirm that the garment described below was professionally cleaned at our premises on 10 June 2026 on behalf of our mutual customer Marguerite Oakley, under our docket B-24118. The garment is a Carla Zampatti navy beaded evening gown, full length with cap sleeves and all-over bugle beading, purchased from your store in October 2023. We have cleaned the same gown twice before, in October 2024 and December 2025, on both occasions without incident.

The care label is intact and legible, sewn into the left side seam. It reads "Dry clean only" and carries a circle containing the letter "P" with a bar beneath it, being a reduced perchloroethylene process. It carries no supplementary warning of any kind relating to the beading. We did not use perchloroethylene. The gown was cleaned in hydrocarbon solvent on our Realstar HM-450, programme 6, which is our beaded and at-risk programme: a four minute bath, no spin above 200 rpm, and drying at 38 degrees C with an extended cool-down. It was bagged in a net with the beading turned inward, run alone rather than with other work, and it was not pressed at any stage. Hydrocarbon on that programme is materially milder than the process the label permits. We selected it because the beads are unlabelled and test as plastic rather than glass, and plastic bugle beads are the component most at risk in any solvent.

On unloading, our plant operator recorded that approximately 15 per cent of the bugle beads across the bodice had lost surface clarity and gone matt. No beads were lost. None of the securing stitching has failed. The polyester ground fabric is entirely unaffected: there is no shrinkage, no distortion, no colour change, no solvent ring and no loss of hand. The change is confined to the surface of the beads themselves, and it is denser on the bodice, where the beading is dense, than on the skirt, where it thins out.

That distribution is the diagnosis. A cleaning fault acts on a garment as a whole and shows first in the ground fabric, the seams and the interlinings. Here the ground is perfect and only one component has altered. The bugle beads carry an applied surface coating, which is what gives a plastic bead its clarity and depth of colour. That coating is bonded to the bead by the bead manufacturer and is not a fabric finish we can test for or condition. Where the bond is weak or the coating has been thinly applied, solvent immersion will craze and lift it, and the bead goes matt while everything around it stays sound. That is a component failure, not a process failure.

DLI TABS — Prints, Embellishments, Trims & Notions addresses this failure mode directly. It records that coated and surface-finished beads, sequins and applied trims may dull, craze, delaminate or dissolve in any professional solvent, that the behaviour depends on the coating chemistry chosen by the trim supplier, and that it cannot be predicted or prevented by a cleaner who has followed the care instructions provided. There is no test available at the counter that distinguishes a sound bead coating from an unsound one. The International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products places responsibility for a component that fails in a process the label permits with the party that selected and specified that component, which is the manufacturer, not the cleaner.

We would also draw your attention to the care labelling. AS/NZS 1957 Textiles — Care Labelling requires that care instructions account for the whole garment, including trim and applied decoration, and that any component requiring different or restricted treatment be identified. This label does not mention the beading at all. Had it carried a warning that the trim was not solvent-stable, or specified a process on account of the beads, the garment would have been declined or handled differently. In our view the inadequacy of the instructions has contributed materially to the outcome.

In summary: the gown was cleaned strictly in accordance with its care label, by a process gentler than that label permits, with every professional precaution available to us, by a plant that has cleaned this garment successfully twice before. It is our professional opinion that the change to the beads results from the failure of the coating applied to the beads at manufacture, and not from the cleaning process.

We have advised Mrs Oakley to return the gown to the original point of purchase for assessment, and we have released it to her for that purpose. Our intake photographs, our post-cycle photographs and the machine record for the cycle are held on file.

If it would assist your assessment or that of the manufacturer, we are happy to provide those records, the full cycle parameters, or a further technical explanation, and you are welcome to contact us directly.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: First written warning — Marco Rossi, daily safety device tests
letters.body:
Dear Marco,

This letter confirms the outcome of our meeting on 10 June 2026 and is a first written warning about the completion of the daily safety device tests on the press line.

The issue is this. Every morning, before the press line is used, the two-hand controls and the guard interlocks on the LP-580 shirt unit, the UP-120 utility press and both trouser machines have to be function-tested and the result written on the weekly test record. That takes about four minutes. It is on the daily start-up checklist and it is a requirement of the manufacturer's own manual, which we hold on file.

On 18 May, 26 May, 2 June and 8 June the test record was left blank for the whole line. On 8 June I watched you start the utility press and begin work without testing anything. When I raised it you said the machines had been fine the day before.

We had talked about this twice already — on 21 April at the toolbox meeting, where I went through the record with the whole plant, and again on 12 May one to one, when you told me you would pick it up. I am putting it in writing now because two conversations have not changed it.

I want to be plain about why this matters rather than just tell you it is a rule. A two-hand control is what stops a press closing on a hand. It fails silently — nothing looks different until the day it does not stop, and by then somebody is in the Bendigo Base emergency department. The test is not paperwork. The record is what proves the test happened.

At the meeting you said you had been under pressure with the volume in May and that the test felt like a delay when there were racks waiting. I accept the volume was heavy. It is not a reason to skip it, and if the workload is genuinely making the start-up impossible then that is something to raise with Sharon or with me so we can move the start time, not something to solve by leaving it out.

What has to change: from Monday 15 June 2026, the daily safety device test is completed on every machine on the press line before any garment is pressed, and the weekly test record is signed each morning. Sharon will check the record daily for the next four weeks and then weekly.

If the tests and the record are not completed as required, further disciplinary action may follow, which could include a final written warning or termination of your employment.

This warning will stay on your file. You were offered a support person for the meeting on 10 June and chose to attend on your own. If you disagree with anything in this letter, put it in writing within seven days and it will be placed on your file alongside it.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Charcoal wool suit jacket — docket B-23904
letters.body:
Dear Trevor,

The colour loss across the collar and shoulders of your jacket is our responsibility and we accept it. You brought the jacket back on 28 May and you were right about what you were looking at. I am not going to put this on the garment.

What happened is this. The collar and the tops of the shoulders are where hair product, skin oil and perspiration concentrate on a jacket, and over three years and four cleans they build up in the fibre. Those residues weaken the dye in that area before we ever touch it. When the garment then goes through a standard perchloroethylene cycle, the solvent lifts the weakened dye along with the soil, and you get exactly what you have: the collar and shoulders two shades lighter than the body, with a defined tide line where the collar meets the jacket. The trousers went through the same load and are unchanged, which tells you the machine was doing what it should. Our own procedure says that a garment showing that kind of collar build-up goes to hydrocarbon or is pre-spotted before it goes anywhere. Neither was done, and the build-up was not recorded at intake. That is the failure, and it is ours.

For what it is worth technically, DLI TABS — Colour Fading & Discoloration sets out the same mechanism: dye weakened by body soils and grooming products fails locally in the next clean, which is why the correct handling is to identify the affected areas at intake and treat them first. We did not.

On the money. Textile claims in Australia are settled on the International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products, which is the standard the trade, insurers and Consumer Affairs all work from. It works on depreciated value rather than replacement cost, because a garment that has been worn and cleaned for three years is not worth what a new one costs. The Guide gives a wool or wool blend suit a normal life expectancy of three years. Yours is 36 months old, which puts it in the 28 to 37 month band, and its condition on the Guide's scale is average — sound and well kept, but three years into a three year life. That band at average condition adjusts to 20 per cent of replacement cost. On a replacement cost of $1,250 for the two-piece suit, that is $250.00.

I know that figure will look low against what you paid, and I would rather say so plainly than dress it up. It is not a valuation of what the suit means to you or a comment on how well you have looked after it. It is what the Guide says the remaining life of a three year old suit is worth, and it is the same calculation we would be held to if this went to Consumer Affairs or to our insurer.

Our offer is $250.00, and we are waiving the cleaning charge of $32.00 for the suit, so nothing is payable to us. If you have already paid it, we will refund it with the settlement.

On payment of the full adjusted value the jacket and trousers become our property, which is the ordinary position under the Guide. If you would rather keep the suit — the trousers are perfectly good and a tailor may be able to do something with the jacket, or you may want it for wear where it does not matter — say so and we will return it to you.

To accept, ring me on (03) 5443 8817 or reply to this letter, and tell me whether you want the suit back. Payment goes out by electronic transfer within five business days of you confirming, to whatever account you nominate, or as a cheque if you prefer.

I am sorry to have cost you a good suit, and I would like the chance to keep looking after your work.

Yours sincerely,

letters.subject: Four pairs lined curtains — docket B-22886
letters.body:
Dear Mrs Kastellorizos,

Thank you for your call of 9 April and for letting Karen come out to the house on 14 April to look at the curtains hung. We have now gone through the docket, the intake measurements and the photographs, and I am writing to set out where we stand.

The four pairs of lined pinch-pleat curtains came in on 30 March, were cleaned on 2 April and were collected on 4 April, under docket B-22886. They were measured at the counter at intake and the measurement written on the docket was 2,650 mm from the top of the pleat to the hem. Measured again at your house on 14 April, the same pairs come to 2,610 mm. The difference is 40 mm, which on a 2,650 mm drop is 1.5 per cent.

That figure is the answer to the question. Relaxation shrinkage of up to 3 per cent is normal in curtains of this construction and is accepted throughout the trade as a fabric characteristic rather than a cleaning fault. Yours are a cotton and linen union face with a cotton sateen lining, made to measure in 2019, with no pre-shrink treatment applied by the maker — your own invoice confirms that — and they had hung for seven years without ever being cleaned. Over that time a hung curtain stretches under its own weight and holds the stretch. The first clean releases it, and the fabric returns towards the length it was woven at. Two natural fibres of different shrinkage behaviour in the face cloth, over a cotton lining, make that movement certain rather than merely possible. At 1.5 per cent, yours have moved half of what the trade allows.

DLI TABS — Stretch, Shrinkage & Distortion sets out the same position: relaxation shrinkage in drapery is an inherent characteristic of the fabric and its history on the rail, it is not caused or prevented by the cleaning process, and it is not a defect in workmanship. Our drapery programme is the mildest cycle we run on a lined curtain — extended bath, reduced mechanical action, 180 rpm extract, dried at 45 degrees C — and they were hung to relax straight out of the machine rather than folded.

This was also put to you in writing before the work began. The drapery advice you signed on 30 March states in terms that relaxation shrinkage of up to 3 per cent is normal and is not a fault, and it covers the risk to sun-weakened fabric as well. That was not a formality; it is there because this happens, and it is why we measure at the counter. The sun degradation along the leading edges of the two north-facing pairs was recorded and photographed at intake, and it is unchanged.

I should also note that the curtains carry no care label of any kind — none was supplied by the maker. Without a care label there is no manufacturer's instruction as to process, temperature or shrinkage allowance, and we handled them on our own judgement, at the mildest setting available to us, having told you in writing what the risk was.

For those reasons we do not accept liability for the change in length, and we are not able to meet the replacement quotation of $2,400.

What we can do is fix the problem. There is turn-up in the hems — Karen checked on 14 April — and 40 mm is well within it. Our alterations room will let all four pairs down to their original 2,650 mm and re-press the hems at our cost. There is no charge for the work and no charge for the pressing. Anh does our alterations and she is in Tuesday to Friday. Bring them in whenever it suits you, or ring us and Dylan will collect them on his next run out your way. Allow about a week.

If you would like to talk any of this through, ring me on (03) 5443 8817. I would much rather have your curtains hanging properly than have this sit between us.

Yours sincerely,

customCourses.title: Tagging garments the Main Street way
customCourses.blurb: How we tag, record and authorise a garment at this counter — the docket, the inspection order, what goes on an at-risk tag, and the conversation you have before the customer walks away.
customCourses.source: SOP 01 — Counter intake, inspection and at-risk tagging, v4

lessons.h: Why the tag is the evidence
lessons.body:
Almost every claim this business has lost, it lost at the counter — not in the plant.

By the time a garment comes back six weeks later, nobody remembers what it looked like when it arrived. What remains is the docket, the tag and the photographs. If those are thin, the customer's account of the garment's condition is the only account there is, and we will be arguing against it with nothing.

So treat the ninety seconds at intake as the most valuable ninety seconds in the job. Two things come out of it:

- **A record** — what the garment was, what was already wrong with it, and what we said we would do.
- **A decision** — whether we take it at all, and on what terms.

Neither can be reconstructed later. Both are cheap now.

lessons.h: The docket, and getting it right first time
lessons.body:
Every garment gets a docket before it leaves the counter. No exceptions, no "I'll do it in a minute".

- **Bendigo dockets are prefixed B-. Kangaroo Flat dockets are prefixed K-.** The prefix travels with the garment, so a K- docket in the Bendigo plant tells the operator it came through the drop store and the intake was done by somebody working alone.
- **Count the pieces out loud, with the customer watching.** A two-piece suit is two pieces. A dress with a separate belt is two pieces. Say the number back to them.
- **Phone number is not optional.** If someone will not give one, write on the docket that they declined and read them the collection date instead. A garment we cannot ring about is a garment that sits on the rack for three months.
- **Collection date** is what we can actually do, not what they would like. If it is going out to the leather specialist, it is three to four weeks and you say so now.

Work the same order every time. Order is what stops you missing things when the shop is busy.

**Collar → shoulders → cuffs → front → back → hem → lining → pockets → closures → trims.**

At each point you are looking for three things: damage that is already there, wear that will become damage, and anything that will not survive the process.

Specifically:

- **Collar and cuffs** — build-up, shine, fraying at the fold. Build-up on a collar changes what machine the garment goes into.
- **Shoulders** — sun fade, which is common in Bendigo and always worse on the side the customer drives with.
- **Pockets** — empty them. Every one. A pen in a pocket is a claim, and it is a claim we cannot defend.
- **Closures and trims** — buttons, zips, beading, sequins, appliqué, anything glued rather than sewn.
- **Lining** — split linings at the underarm are so common that not recording one is negligent.

Use the daylight lamp at the end of the counter, not the overhead fluorescents. Take a garment to the window if you are unsure.

A garment is at-risk if any of these are true. This is not a judgement call — if it is on the list, it is at-risk.

- Beading, sequins, or any applied embellishment
- Applied print, foil, flock or transfer
- Polyurethane, coated, bonded or fused construction
- Leather or suede, including trim on an otherwise ordinary garment
- Faux fur
- **No care label**, or a label that is cut out, illegible, or contradicts the fabric
- The garment is more than about five years old
- A wedding gown, or any made-to-measure formal
- Curtains, in every case
- It is already damaged, stained or worn through
- **The customer tells you it is precious.** Their word for it counts.

Each of those fails in its own way. Beads cloud and lose their coating. Prints crack and lift. Bonded fabrics delaminate. Coated fabrics go tacky. None of it can be predicted from looking, and none of it is our fault when it happens — but only if we said so first.

The at-risk conversation is the part people avoid, because it sounds like telling a customer their garment might get wrecked. Done properly it does the opposite: it tells them we know what we are looking at.

Something close to this works:

> "I want to point something out before I take this. The beading here is plastic rather than glass, and plastic beading sometimes goes cloudy in solvent — it's the coating on the bead, not the cleaning. I'll run it on the gentlest machine we have, but I can't promise the beads. Are you happy for me to go ahead on that basis?"

Then:

- **The authorisation is signed before we accept the garment. Never after.** An authorisation signed when the customer comes to collect is worth nothing at all.
- Name the specific risk on the form. "At-risk garment" on its own means nothing. "Plastic bugle beading may cloud, dull or lose surface" is a record.
- **Photograph it.** Minimum four for anything at-risk, with a scale reference, and close-ups of whatever you have just written down.
- If they push back, or if you are not sure, we would rather decline the garment than take one we cannot clean safely. Nobody will ever be in trouble for declining.

And at Kangaroo Flat, working alone: **photograph, ring Bendigo, and do not accept an at-risk garment on your own judgement.**

quiz.q: A customer brings in a dress with plastic sequins across the bodice. What is the correct sequence?
a: Take it, clean it on the gentlest cycle, and mention the risk if she asks
Explain the risk, have her sign the at-risk authorisation, photograph it, then accept it
Decline it — sequinned garments are never accepted
Accept it and note "at-risk" on the docket
quiz.why: The authorisation is signed before the garment is accepted, the specific risk is named, and it is photographed. Noting "at-risk" on the docket without a signature and without naming the risk is not a record of anything.

quiz.q: What does a K- prefix on a docket tell the plant operator?
a: The garment is a knitwear item
The garment came through the Kangaroo Flat drop store
The garment is for a commercial account
The garment needs a specialist clean
quiz.why: K- is Kangaroo Flat, B- is Bendigo. It matters because the drop store is staffed by one person working alone, so the intake decision there was made without a second opinion.

quiz.q: In what order do you inspect a garment?
a: Whatever order the garment suggests
Front, back, then anything that looks unusual
Collar, shoulders, cuffs, front, back, hem, lining, pockets, closures, trims
Pockets first, then the rest by eye
quiz.why: The same order every time is what stops you missing things when the shop is busy. Working by eye means you find what catches your attention, not what is actually there.

quiz.q: A jacket has no care label at all. What follows?
a: Clean it as you would any similar fabric
It is automatically an at-risk garment
Refuse it outright
Ask the customer what the label said and write that down
quiz.why: No label, a cut-out label, an illegible label or a label that contradicts the fabric all put the garment on the at-risk list. It may still be accepted — on a signed authorisation.

quiz.q: When may an at-risk authorisation be signed?
a: Any time before the garment is collected
Before the garment is accepted, and only then
At collection, when the customer can see the result
Whenever the customer next comes in
quiz.why: Before acceptance. An authorisation signed afterwards records nothing about the decision the customer actually made, and will not survive being tested.

quiz.q: A customer says the dress is not valuable but that it was her mother’s. Is it at-risk?
a: No — value is what decides it
Only if it is also over five years old
Yes — the customer telling you it is precious puts it on the list
Only if it has beading or a coating
quiz.why: Their word for it counts. What a garment is worth to the person standing in front of you is not the same as what it is worth, and it is the first thing that decides how a complaint goes.

quiz.q: You are alone at Kangaroo Flat and a customer brings in a beaded gown. What do you do?
a: Photograph it, ring Bendigo, and do not accept it on your own judgement
Take it on an at-risk authorisation as you would at Bendigo
Decline it and send the customer to Bendigo
Accept it and flag it for the driver to raise
quiz.why: Working alone means there is no second opinion available, so the rule is explicit: photograph, ring Bendigo, and let the decision be made with someone else’s eyes on it.

quiz.q: Why does build-up on a collar change anything?
a: It does not — it comes out in any machine
It means the garment must be declined
It changes which machine the garment goes into, or means it is pre-spotted first
It only matters on white shirts
quiz.why: Product and perspiration build-up weakens the dye underneath it. Our procedure sends that garment to hydrocarbon or has it pre-spotted. Skipping that step is how the Lindsay suit jacket came back two shades lighter across the collar.

documents.title: Union XL-800 manual — Dry Cleaning Machine — Operations and Maintenance Manual, Installation and services required, Running a cycle
documents.background: The 25 kg perc machine in the Bendigo plant, installed March 2019, serial UXL8-2019-0447. Manual revision 4, January 2024. This is the machine most of our volume goes through.
documents.text:
# UNION XL-800

## Dry Cleaning Machine — Operations and Maintenance Manual

**Model:** XL-800
**Machine type:** Enclosed-circuit dry-to-dry perchloroethylene dry cleaning machine, three-tank, with integrated distillation still and refrigerated solvent recovery
**Nominal load capacity:** 25 kg
**Serial number:** UXL8-2019-0447
**Year of manufacture:** 2018
**Date of installation:** March 2019
**Installed at:** Main Street Dry Cleaners, Shop 4, 118 Hargreaves Street, Bendigo VIC 3550
**Manual revision:** Rev 4, January 2024. Supersedes Rev 3, June 2021.

### Revision history

| Rev | Date | Summary of change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 03/2017 | First issue for XL-800 series. |
| 2 | 11/2018 | Added refrigerated recovery data; revised fault codes E24 to E27. |
| 3 | 06/2021 | Revised exposure-limit references; added programmes 11 and 12; added E34 and E40. |
| 4 | 01/2024 | Revised maintenance intervals; added carbon adsorber desorb procedure; expanded fault code section; corrected still steam demand; added decommissioning notes. |

---

## 1. Front matter

### 1.1 About this manual

This manual covers the installation, operation, routine maintenance and fault
diagnosis of the Union XL-800 three-tank perchloroethylene dry cleaning machine.
It is written for the machine owner, the trained plant operator, and the
technician who attends the machine for scheduled service.

### 1.2 How to use this manual

- **New to the machine:** read Section 2 (Safety) and Section 5 (Machine
  description) before touching the control panel, then Section 8.
- **Running the machine day to day:** Sections 7, 8, 9 and 10. Keep a copy of
  the programme table near the panel.
- **Machine stopped with a code displayed:** go straight to Section 11. The
  table says whether an operator may clear the fault or whether a technician is
  required. If it says technician, stop and call one.
- **Ordering parts:** Section 12. Quote serial UXL8-2019-0447 with every order.
- **Quoting service work:** Section 13 sets out intervals and what voids
  warranty.

### 1.3 Symbols used in this manual

| Symbol word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DANGER** | A hazard that will cause death or serious injury if the instruction is not followed. |
| **WARNING** | A hazard that may cause death or serious injury if the instruction is not followed. |
| **CAUTION** | A hazard that may cause minor injury, or that will damage the machine. |
| **NOTE** | Information that affects the result of the work but is not a hazard. |
| **TECHNICIAN** | The task must be done by a person holding the relevant trade licence or the manufacturer's service authorisation. An operator must not attempt it. |

### 1.4 Machine identification

The machine data plate is fixed to the right-hand side panel, 1,500 mm above
floor level, adjacent to the electrical isolator. It carries the model, serial
number, year of manufacture, supply voltage, full load current, solvent charge,
refrigerant type and charge mass, and the maximum working pressure of the still
steam jacket. Do not remove, paint over or obscure the data plate. If it becomes
unreadable, order a replacement by quoting the serial number.

A second plate on the still access panel carries the still vessel number, the
design pressure of the steam jacket and the date of the last internal inspection.

### 1.5 Intended use

The XL-800 is designed to clean textile garments and made-up textile articles in
perchloroethylene in a closed circuit, and to recover the solvent from the load
by heated air drying, refrigerated condensation and carbon adsorption.

The machine must not be used:

- with any solvent other than perchloroethylene, unless converted by the
  manufacturer and re-plated accordingly;
- to clean articles contaminated with flammable liquids, oxidising agents, paint,
  adhesive, or unknown chemical residues;
- to clean articles carrying free water above the limit at 8.3;
- to dry articles that have not been through a solvent bath in this machine;
- as a storage vessel for solvent outside the machine's own tanks.

### 1.6 Residual risks

Even when the machine is used as intended and all guards are fitted, the
following risks remain and must be managed by the occupier:

- solvent vapour exposure during button trap and lint trap opening;
- solvent vapour and hot surfaces during still cleaning;
- hot condensate and steam at the still jacket and the drying battery;
- rotating drum inertia after the drive is de-energised;
- stored energy in the compressed air receiver and the refrigeration circuit;
- manual handling of muck drums, filter cartridges and solvent drums.
