## 6. UP-120 utility press

### 6.1 Description

The UP-120 is a steam-heated utility press with a fixed lower buck and a
pneumatically driven upper head, initiated by a two-hand control. It is the
general-purpose press on the line and it does the work the shaped machines cannot:
jackets, skirts, the final touch on trousers, and anything odd.

Two bucks are supplied and are interchangeable in about ten minutes by a supervisor.
The **rectangular** buck (1,100 × 330 mm) is used for flat work — skirt panels,
trouser finishing, sleeves, hems. The **mushroom** buck (620 × 300 mm, crowned 40 mm)
is used for shaped work — jacket shoulders, sleeve heads, collars, the seat of a
skirt. Working shaped garments on the flat buck is the most common cause of seam
impression on this line.

The head is steam heated to 160–170 °C and the buck to 118–124 °C under its cover.
Buck vacuum is drawn through the perforated buck face and is controlled by a foot
pedal independently of the head, so the operator can set a garment with vacuum before
the head is brought down and can hold it with vacuum after the head lifts. Head
pressure is set at the regulator on the right-hand side of the frame and read on the
panel gauge.

### 6.2 Head and buck padding

| Layer | Material | Thickness | Part |
|---|---|---|---|
| Head face | Needled Nomex felt | 6 mm | SK-120-PAD-H5 |
| Head cover | Silicone-treated Nomex cloth | 1 mm | SK-120-COV-H5 |
| Buck base pad | Spring steel mesh | 12 mm | SK-120-MSH-B2 |
| Buck upper pad | Needled polyester felt, perforated | 10 mm | SK-120-PAD-B5 |
| Buck cover | Cotton drill, shrink-fit | 0.8 mm | SK-120-COV-B5 |
| Mushroom buck pad | Moulded felt | 14 mm | SK-120-PAD-M5 |
| Mushroom buck cover | Cotton drill, shrink-fit | 0.8 mm | SK-120-COV-M5 |

Padding does three jobs: it spreads the closing force so the garment is not marked by
the metal, it lets steam and vacuum pass, and it absorbs the thickness of a seam so
that the seam is not pressed through to the face. A flattened pad does none of these
and produces seam impression, shine and uneven drying at the same time. See 9.3.

### 6.3 The four common uses

**Jackets.** Mushroom buck. Work the garment in sections and never press a whole
front at once. Order: back, then shoulders and sleeve heads on the crown, then
fronts, then lapels last with the head off — lapels are rolled with steam and hand
pressure, not pressed flat. Never press a jacket with the lining pulled tight;
release it and let it sit. Do not press over a shoulder pad edge; move the garment so
the pad edge sits off the crown. Finish the collar on the crown with the collar
rolled, not flattened.

**Skirts.** Rectangular buck for panels and hems; mushroom buck for the seat and for
any shaping at the hip. Pleated skirts are set pleat by pleat with the head just
kissing the cloth, not at full closure. A lined skirt is pressed from the face with
the lining hanging free. Waistbands are done last on the rectangular buck.

**Trouser finishing.** The UP-120 finishes what the TT-240 and TL-260 leave: the
waistband, the fly, the pocket bags and the top of the seat if the topper has left a
mark. Use the mushroom buck for the seat and the rectangular buck for the waistband.
Do not use the UP-120 to set a crease; that is the legger's job, and a crease set by
hand on this press will not match the machine crease.

**General.** Aprons, tablecloths, uniform shirts too large for the LP-580, overalls,
curtains and anything flat. For long flat work, press in overlapping passes of about
900 mm and move the garment between passes rather than dragging it under a closed
head.

### 6.4 Pressure and time settings by fabric class

| Class | Fabrics | Head pressure | Steam | Vacuum | Buck vacuum before close |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Silk, acetate, fine viscose, chiffon | 180 kPa | 1.5 s | 6 s | Yes |
| 2 | Fine wool, worsted suiting under 240 g/m² | 260 kPa | 2.0 s | 8 s | Yes |
| 3 | Worsted suiting 240–320 g/m², wool blends | 340 kPa | 3.0 s | 8 s | Yes |
| 4 | Cotton, linen, drill, poly-cotton | 480 kPa | 4.0 s | 10 s | Optional |
| 5 | Heavy wool, tweed, coating, denim | 620 kPa | 5.0 s | 12 s | No |
| 6 | Synthetic knit, polyester, acrylic | 200 kPa | 1.0 s | 10 s | Yes |

Full closing force of 26 kN corresponds to 620 kPa; class 2 at 260 kPa gives about
11 kN. Where a garment carries two fabrics — a wool jacket with a synthetic lining,
for example — set to the lower class.

**CAUTION** — Class 6 synthetics melt. Polyester begins to glaze at 150 °C and the
head runs at 165 °C. Always use a press cloth on synthetics and never dwell.

documents.text:
### 6.5 Avoiding shine on worsted and on dark fabrics

Shine is flattened, polished fibre. On worsted and on dark cloth it is the single
most common complaint and, once it is severe, it is not fully recoverable.

Causes, in order of how often they are the actual cause:

1. Too much head pressure for the cloth class.
2. Pressing from the face without a press cloth.
3. A flattened or glazed head cover, which is hard and smooth instead of soft and
   matt.
4. Dwelling — leaving the head closed after the steam and vacuum have finished.
5. Pressing a dry garment. Steam is what lets the fibre move; without it the head
   simply crushes the surface.
6. Pressing over a seam, a pocket bag or a shoulder pad edge, which concentrates the
   whole force on a narrow line.

Prevention:

- Drop one pressure class from what the fabric weight suggests.
- Press from the reverse wherever the garment construction allows it.
- Where the face must be pressed, use a press cloth (6.6) without exception.
- Use steam and vacuum to do the work and use pressure only to hold the cloth still.
  On a class 2 or 3 garment the head should be firm, not hard.
- Open the head as soon as vacuum ends.
- Finish with a short steam-only pass with the head 20 mm off the cloth, then vacuum,
  to lift the surface.
- Replace the head cover on schedule. A glazed cover will shine a garment at any
  pressure setting.

Recovery of light shine: steam the area from the reverse with the head off, brush the
nap up with a soft brush while damp, and vacuum flat. Severe shine where the fibre
has been fused is permanent.

### 6.6 Using a press cloth

A press cloth is a piece of unbleached cotton or wool flannel laid between the head
and the garment. It diffuses the heat, absorbs some of the pressure, and stops the
head cover contacting the face of the cloth.

| Cloth | Material | Size | Use | Part |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| General | Unbleached cotton drill | 900 × 400 mm | Cotton, linen, synthetics | SK-GEN-PRC-1 |
| Wool | Wool flannel | 700 × 350 mm | Worsted, wool, dark suiting | SK-GEN-PRC-2 |
| Fine | Silk organza | 500 × 300 mm | Silk, acetate, fine viscose | SK-GEN-PRC-3 |

Use it dry unless the garment is bone dry, in which case dampen it evenly and never
in patches — a patchy damp cloth is the most common cause of water spotting on this
press. Keep press cloths clean; a cloth with a mark on it will transfer that mark
under heat. Wash them weekly and discard any that has gone stiff or shiny.

### 6.7 Pad and cover change procedure

**TECHNICIAN or trained supervisor. Not an operator task.**

1. Isolate steam, air and electricity under 2.8. Allow 40 minutes cooling. A head
   cover cannot be fitted correctly to a hot head in any case.
2. Release the buck cover drawstring at the underside and remove the old cover. Note
   which way the seam ran.
3. Lift out the upper felt pad and inspect the spring mesh below. Mesh that has
   collapsed anywhere across the buck is replaced at the same time.
4. Vacuum the buck face and clear every perforation. Blocked perforations after a pad
   change are the reason a freshly re-padded press sometimes dries worse than it did
   before.
5. Lay the new felt pad, perforated side matching the buck, and smooth it from the
   centre out. Do not stretch it.
6. Fit the new cover damp, pull the drawstring evenly, and work the wrinkles out from
   the centre. Tie off and tuck the cord clear of the buck edge.
7. For the head: remove the four M8 retaining clips, lift the old cover and felt off,
   clean the head face with the cleaning block, fit the new felt, then the cover, and
   re-clip. The cover must be taut with no wrinkle at the nose of the head.
8. Restore services, run three empty cycles at class 4 settings to shrink and set the
   covers, then press a scrap garment and check for wrinkle transfer.
9. Record the change in Appendix C.

### 6.8 Changing between bucks

**Supervisor task.** Isolate under 2.8 and allow the buck to cool. Disconnect the buck
steam union and the vacuum spigot, remove the four M10 buck retaining bolts, lift the
buck clear with two people, seat the replacement on its gasket, refit and torque the
bolts to 45 Nm, reconnect the union and spigot, restore services and check for leaks
at working pressure before the first garment. Do not use a buck whose gasket has been
disturbed more than three times; order a new gasket set with the change.

---

## 7. TT-240 trouser topper and TL-260 legger

### 7.1 Description

The two machines finish a pair of trousers between them. The **TT-240** finishes the
top: waistband, seat, fly, pleats and the top 300 mm of each leg. The **TL-260**
finishes the legs and sets the creases.

The TT-240 has an expanding waist clamp that opens from 700 mm to 1,250 mm, a heated
seat plate 480 × 420 mm, a fly plate, and twin vacuum. The trousers are dressed
waist-down over the form, the waist clamp expands to take up the slack, steam is
admitted, and vacuum sets the finish. There is no contact pressing on the seat except
where the seat plate closes.

The TL-260 has two heated leg bucks 1,150 × 260 mm and an automatic clamp sequence.
The legs are laid on the bucks with the creases aligned, the clamps close at up to
6.8 kN, steam and vacuum follow, and the crease is set by the clamp line falling
exactly on the fold.

Worked as a pair by one operator, the two machines produce 40–46 finished pairs an
hour. Topping is faster than legging, so the operator tops two pairs while the legger
runs one.

### 7.2 Crease-setting sequence

1. Turn the trousers right side out and check the pockets are empty and flat.
2. **Top first.** Dress onto the TT-240, waist over the form, fly to the front guide,
   back seam centred on the seat plate. Close the waist clamp on the two-hand control.
   Run the cycle. Remove.
3. **Match the legs.** Hold the trousers by the waistband, let them hang, and bring
   the inside leg seams together. The trousers will settle into their own creases. Do
   not force a new crease line.
4. **Lay the front leg.** Place the front of both legs on the TL-260 bucks, front
   crease running down the centre of each buck, cuff or hem to the end stop.
5. Check that the fly is flat, that the pocket bags are not folded under, and that
   the crease is straight for the whole length. A crease that wanders here will be set
   where it wanders.
6. Initiate. Clamps close, steam 6 s, vacuum 14 s, clamps open.
7. **Turn and repeat for the back.** Same alignment, back crease centred.
8. Hang immediately on a clamp hanger. A pair left folded over a rail while warm will
   take a second crease from the rail.

### 7.3 Clamp settings

| Setting | TT-240 waist clamp | TL-260 leg clamp | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.8 kN | 2.8 kN | Silk, fine viscose, unlined summer trousers |
| 2 | 2.6 kN | 4.0 kN | Fine worsted, tropical weight wool |
| 3 | 3.4 kN | 5.4 kN | Standard worsted suiting, poly-wool |
| 4 | 4.4 kN | 6.8 kN | Cotton drill, moleskin, heavy wool, denim |

Waist clamp expansion is set by the WAIST control in 50 mm steps. Set it to the
garment before dressing, not after; expanding a clamp against a fastened waistband
will pop a button or split a seam.

### 7.4 Setting a crease on a cuffed trouser

A turn-up changes where the crease stops and how the hem is handled.

1. Do not press the crease through the turn-up. The crease stops at the top edge of
   the turn-up, and the turn-up itself is pressed flat and square.
2. Set the TL-260 hem stop to the top of the turn-up, not to the bottom of the
   trouser, using the sliding stop on each buck.
3. Press the leg as normal. The turn-up hangs past the clamp line.
4. Finish the turn-up on the UP-120 rectangular buck at one class below the leg
   setting, with the turn-up opened flat and the fold pressed only at the outer edge.
5. Re-fold the turn-up, check both legs are the same length by laying them together,
   and give it a two-second set with the head kissing the fold.

Unequal turn-ups are the most common complaint on cuffed trousers and are almost
always caused by pressing them separately rather than together.

### 7.5 Handling pleats

- Identify the pleat type before you start. A **forward pleat** folds towards the
  fly, a **reverse pleat** away from it. Setting a pleat the wrong way round is not
  recoverable in one press; the old fold shows.
- On the TT-240, set each pleat by hand on the form before closing the waist clamp,
  and hold it with the pleat pins provided (SK-240-PIN-2).
- Do not press a pleat below the point where the manufacturer's original press
  stopped, usually 150–200 mm below the waistband. A pleat carried too far down reads
  as a crease in the wrong place.
- Double pleats are set outer first, then inner.
- On unlined trousers, check the pocket bag is not caught in the pleat fold.

### 7.6 Permanent press versus wool

| Property | Permanent press / poly blend | Wool and worsted |
|---|---|---|
| Programme | Standard, 25 s TT / 32 s TL | Wool, 34 s TT / 40 s TL |
| Clamp setting | 3 | 2 or 3 |
| Steam | Short, 3 s | Longer, 6 s |
| Vacuum | Long, 14–16 s | Long, 16 s, and let it cool on the buck |
| Temperature limit | 150 °C — resin scorches and yellows | 160 °C |
| Crease durability | Very high; an old crease is hard to remove | Moderate; sets and resets readily |
| Main risk | Glazing and shine at the crease | Shrinkage and seam impression |

Wool must be allowed to cool under vacuum before it comes off the buck. Wool sets its
shape as it cools, not while it is hot. A pair taken off warm will drop its crease
within a day, and the customer will report that the crease "didn't last". The wool
programme's longer vacuum exists for exactly this reason and must not be trimmed to
speed the line up.

Permanent press trousers hold whatever crease is put into them, including a wrong
one. Check the alignment twice before initiating on a poly blend.

### 7.7 Common finishing faults on the topper and legger

| Fault | Cause | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Double crease down the leg | Legs not matched to the original crease before laying; or the pair re-legged after being folded warm | Damp out the old crease, cool, re-lay and re-press |
| Crease off-centre at the cuff | Hem not to the end stop; one leg pulled longer than the other | Re-lay both legs together to the stop |
| Waistband marked or ridged | Waist clamp setting too high, or waistband not seated flat on the form | Drop a setting; reseat and re-run |
| Seat shine | Seat plate pressure too high on worsted | Press from the reverse or drop a clamp setting; see 6.5 for recovery |
| Pocket bag impression on the front | Pocket bag folded under | Smooth pockets before dressing; re-steam and re-press |
| Crease fades within a day | Wool taken off the buck warm | Extend vacuum; let it cool on the buck |
| Fly puckering | Fly plate closing on a fly that is not fully done up and flat | Do the fly up, flatten, re-run |
| Leg wrinkled behind the knee | Leg not pulled straight along the buck before clamping | Re-lay and re-press |
| Shine at the crease on poly blend | Clamp setting 4 on permanent press | Drop to setting 3; light shine may lift with steam from the reverse |

---

## 8. Finishing quality faults

This is the section to use when a garment comes back. Identify the fault by what it
looks like, not by what the customer says caused it. Where a fault is recoverable,
recover it before the garment goes back to the counter, and record the cause so the
same fault does not go out again the same week.

| Fault | What it looks like | Cause | Prevention | Recoverable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Shine** | Polished, flattened, lighter-looking patch — worst on shoulders, seat, elbows, lapels and dark worsted | Too much pressure for the class; no press cloth; glazed head cover; dwelling; pressing dry cloth; pressing over a seam or pad edge | Drop a fabric class; press from the reverse; always use a press cloth on dark worsted; replace head cover on schedule; open the head as soon as vacuum ends | Light shine usually — steam from the reverse, brush the nap up while damp, vacuum flat. Fused shine is permanent |
| **Seam impression** | Outline of a seam, pocket bag, dart or zip showing through on the face | Pad flattened or too thin; flat buck used for shaped work; too much pressure | Renew buck padding on schedule; mushroom buck for shaped work; seam roll or hand press for thick seams | Usually — re-steam from the reverse and re-press on soft padding without closing on the seam line |
| **Double crease** | Two parallel creases in a trouser leg or a sleeve | Garment re-pressed without removing the first crease; legs not matched; garment folded while warm | Match legs to the original crease before laying; hang immediately; damp down and remove an old crease before setting a new one | Usually — damp the area, steam the old crease out with the head off, allow to cool, then re-press. Permanent press blends may not fully release |
| **Water spotting** | Ring-shaped or irregular pale marks, sometimes with a darker edge, on silk, acetate, viscose and some wools | Condensate spitting from a head or hose; a patchily damp press cloth; steaming a garment that is already too wet; a failed trap letting water into the header | Blow the head through before the first press of the day; test traps quarterly; damp press cloths evenly; check the separator | Sometimes — feather out with steam from the reverse and dry evenly, or return to the wet side. Acetate spotting is often permanent |
| **Scorch** | Yellow, tan or brown discolouration in the shape of the head or buck; the fibre feels crisp | Head or plate temperature too high for the fibre; dwelling; a synthetic pressed without a press cloth; a resin-finished shirt run on a cotton programme | Match the programme to the fibre; never dwell; press cloth on all synthetics and non-iron; verify plate temperatures monthly | No. Light yellowing on cotton sometimes lifts with a bleach bath at the wet side; anything that has changed the fibre is permanent |
| **Flattened nap** | Velvet, corduroy, moleskin or brushed wool looks crushed and shows the direction of the press | Any contact pressing on a napped cloth | Never press a napped fabric on the UP-120. Finish on the Trevil steam-air finisher, or steam with the head off and brush | Often — steam from the reverse with no contact and brush the pile up while damp |
| **Pressed-in stain** | A mark that was there before, now darker, sharper-edged and immovable | The garment went to the press with a stain in it. Heat set it | Inspect every garment before it reaches a press. Stained garments go to the reject rail, not through the machine. See 5.10 | Rarely. Protein and sugar stains set hard under heat. Tell the counter before it goes back |
| **Collar puckering** | The collar leaf ripples along the seam, or the fusing bubbles | Fused collar over-steamed; uneven collar clamp gap; leaf not smoothed flat before clamping; wet steam from low header pressure | Programme B collar values on fused collars; clamp gap set to 0.3 mm; smooth the leaf before clamping; keep header pressure up | Bubbled fusing, no. Simple puckering, yes — re-damp and re-press with less steam and a longer vacuum |
| **Colour change under heat** | A patch a different shade from the rest, often on a dark garment, sometimes visible only in daylight | Heat-sensitive dye — acetate, some reactive dyes, cheap dark cottons; excessive plate temperature; steam and pressure together on a marginal dye | Test an inside seam on any unfamiliar dark garment; drop a class; use a press cloth; keep plate temperatures at the low end of the range | No. This is a dye and fibre change, not a surface effect |
| **Glazing at the crease** | The crease line looks shiny and hard on a poly blend | Permanent press cloth pressed too hot with too much clamp force | Clamp setting 3 maximum on permanent press; keep the TL-260 buck at the low end of 140–150 °C | Rarely — light glazing may lift with steam from the reverse |
| **Damp garment at the hanger** | Feels cool and heavy; creases within an hour in the bag | Vacuum time too short; blocked lint filter; blocked buck perforations; failed steam trap | Extend vacuum before extending steam; clean lint filters weekly; clear perforations at every pad change | Yes — re-run a vacuum-only cycle |
| **Cracked or melted buttons** | Chipped, clouded or flattened buttons, mostly on shirts | Button pressed directly under a head or a clamp bar | Position buttons off the clamp line; check cuffs before closing the cuff bars; use the button clearance channel on the collar plate | No. Replace the button |
| **Lining pulled and rippled** | Jacket or skirt lining shows drag lines and does not sit flat | Pressed with the lining under tension, or pressed through the lining from the face | Release the lining and let it sit before pressing; press the shell from the reverse | Usually — re-steam the lining with the head off and let it hang |
| **Shrinkage on wool** | Garment measurably shorter or tighter, felted handle | Too much steam with too much pressure, or repeated re-pressing of a wet wool garment | Wool programme; let the garment cool under vacuum; do not re-press wet wool repeatedly | No |

---

### 9.2 The effect of a worn cover on finish quality

A cover is not decoration. It is the last 1 mm between a hot metal surface and the
customer's garment, and it controls three things: how heat reaches the cloth, how
steam and vacuum pass through it, and whether the garment picks up a mark.

A worn cover causes, in the order the symptoms usually appear:

1. **Slower drying**, because the fibres have matted and the cover no longer passes
   air. The operator compensates by adding vacuum time and the line slows.
2. **Shine**, because the surface has glazed hard and smooth.
3. **Uneven finish**, because the wear is never even across the buck.
4. **Marking**, because a glazed cover picks up soil from garments and transfers it.
5. **Scorch**, because heat now reaches the cloth faster than the operator expects.

### 9.3 When to change a cover or a pad

Change a **cover** when any of the following is true, regardless of the calendar: it
is shiny or slick to the touch anywhere; it has a hole, a burn, a tear or a permanent
mark; the weave of the felt shows through; a garment picks up the cover's texture; or
drying time has crept up more than 15% with no other explanation.

**Padding** lasts longer than covers but fails less obviously. Test it: press a folded
scrap of heavy cotton with a thick seam in it at class 4. If the seam shows on the
face, the pad is finished. Also change padding when the felt can be compressed to less
than half its original thickness by thumb pressure, when drying is uneven across the
buck, or when the pad has a permanent depression where garments are habitually placed.

Never fit a new cover over old, flattened padding. The cover will not sit flat, it
will wear out early, and the finish will not improve.

### 9.4 Recommended stock holding

The stock column in 9.1 assumes 600 shirts and about 400 other garments a week. The
critical items — the ones that stop the line if they are not on the shelf — are the
LP-580 collar plate cover, the UP-120 head and buck covers, the TL-260 leg buck cover
pair, and the vacuum lint filters. Keep those on the shelf at all times. The spring
mesh, the buck gasket set and the seal kits are ordered against a planned job, not
held.

---

### 10.7 Steam trap testing

A failed trap is the most common cause of a whole-line finishing complaint. Test each
trap with an ultrasonic tester or, failing that, with a contact pyrometer either side
of the trap.

| Symptom | Diagnosis | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous discharge, no cycling | Trap blown open | Replace. It is dumping live steam and pressurising the common return |
| Cold both sides | Trap blocked closed | Clear the strainer, then replace if it stays cold |
| Inlet hot, outlet cold, cycling every 20–60 s | Normal | None |
| Return line hotter than 100 °C along its length | One or more traps blown | Test each in turn |
| Trap cycling continuously at high frequency | Undersized or worn seat | Replace on the next service |

A blown trap on the UP-120 will make the LP-580 finish badly. Test all four before
concluding that a machine has a fault of its own.

### 10.8 Vacuum motors and filters

Blower current draw is the quickest health check. A blower drawing more than 15%
above its commissioning figure has a bearing problem or a blocked exhaust. Record the
reading each quarter so the trend is visible.

Lint filters are cleaned weekly and replaced six-monthly. A filter that has been
washed more than ten times has lost its efficiency and should be replaced regardless
of appearance. Blocked filters degrade the finish long before they raise a fault code,
so a complaint of damp garments with no code on the panel is a filter complaint until
proved otherwise.

### 10.9 Air filter, regulator and lubricator

Each drop has its own FRL, set to the machine's regulated pressure from 3.3. The bowl
is drained daily by the operator. Filter elements are replaced quarterly. Lubricator
drip rate is one drop every 30 cycles; more than that carries oil onto the garment and
shows as spotting, and less than that leads to sticking cylinders and clamp faults.
The compressor receiver is drained daily and the refrigerated dryer checked weekly.
Water in the air line is the cause of most intermittent clamp faults on the TT-240 and
TL-260, and of the seasonal pattern described in 11.5.

"Technician: Yes" means an operator must not attempt the repair. Isolate the machine

### 11.5 Troubleshooting the eight most common faults

**SU-01 / UP-01 / TT-01 / TL-01 — low steam.** Nearly always the first hour of the
day, and nearly always the header rather than the machine. The boiler makes pressure
quickly; the header takes longer to warm and, until it does, it condenses everything
you put into it. Warm the header for ten minutes on the warming valve before opening
the main. If a low-steam code appears mid-morning with the boiler at pressure, the
cause is a blocked Y-strainer on that machine's drop or a blown trap somewhere on the
line pressurising the common return. Blow the strainer down, then test the traps under
10.7. If low steam appears only when all four machines cycle together, the header
volume is short and the line must be sequenced rather than run flat out — top and leg
trousers while the shirt unit is idle, not alongside it.

**SU-03 / UP-02 / TT-02 / TL-02 — low air.** Check the compressor first: running, not
in fault, receiver up. If the compressor is fine and one machine alone is showing the
code, the fault is at that machine's FRL. A filter element at the end of its life will
pass enough air to hold pressure at rest and not enough to hold it during a cycle, so
the gauge looks correct until the machine moves. Change the element. If several
machines show the code together at the same time of day, the compressor duty is being
exceeded, usually because a leak has opened up in the ring main overnight; listen
along the main with the plant quiet before the first shift.

**SU-04 / UP-03 / TT-03 / TL-03 — vacuum failure.** Clean the lint filter before
anything else; it is the cause four times out of five. If the filter is clean, check
the exhaust is not obstructed, then check the blower is turning. A blower that hums
but does not turn has a seized bearing or a failed capacitor and is a technician job.
A blower that trips its overload twice in a day must not be reset a third time. Note
that a vacuum problem usually shows up first as poor finishing rather than as a code
— a partially blocked filter degrades the finish long before it trips the pressure
switch, so treat "damp garments, no code" as a vacuum complaint.

**SU-06 / UP-05 — two-hand control fault.** In most cases the operator has pressed one
button before the other by more than half a second, which is a technique problem, not
a machine problem. Both palms go down together. If the code persists when two
different people have both operated the machine correctly, the fault is in the
control: a sticking button, a worn contact block, or a channel discrepancy detected by
the safety relay. **Do not try to work around this code.** It exists to tell you that
a safety circuit is not behaving as designed. The machine stays out of service until a
technician has tested and, if necessary, replaced the button assembly, and the result
is recorded in Appendix B.

**SU-07 — body former cycle timeout.** The body step has run past 45 s without
reaching its setpoints. Three causes, in order of likelihood: a split former skin,
which will also show SU-10; low steam, which will also show SU-01; and a blocked
vacuum path, which will also show SU-04. If SU-07 appears on its own, inspect the skin
closely at the shoulder and under the arms, where splits start. A skin with a split
will still inflate to a point and will still finish shirts badly, so operators often
run for weeks with a marginal skin and blame the programme. Replacement is an annual
task under 10.5 and takes about 90 minutes.

**SU-13 / SU-14 / TT-09 / TL-09 — jam detected.** Something was between a clamp and
its buck. The usual objects are a cuff button, a collar stay, a hanger hook, a folded
double cuff, a doubled-over collar band, and on the trouser machines a belt buckle or
coins left in a pocket. Isolate under 2.9 before touching anything. Once the
obstruction is out, inspect the cover at the jam point: a button crushed against a
cover leaves a dent that will mark every garment after it. Frequent SU-14 on the
collar station means collars are being loaded without checking for stays; make the
check part of the loading routine at 5.4.

**UP-06 / SU-08 / TL-07 — over-temperature.** The head, plate or buck has exceeded its
limit. This is a real hazard, not a nuisance code: at 185 °C the UP-120 head will
scorch cotton on contact and melt synthetics instantly. The usual cause is a blown
steam trap letting live steam through continuously instead of cycling. Do not reset
and continue. Close the steam valve to that element, allow 40 minutes, and have the
trap tested under 10.7. Check the last garments pressed before the code appeared —
they may be scorched without it being obvious until the customer sees them in
daylight.

**TT-05 / TL-05 — clamp fault.** Look at the pattern before you look at the machine.
If the fault appears in the first hour on cold mornings and disappears later, the
cause is condensate in the air line reaching the clamp cylinders; drain the receiver,
check the refrigerated dryer, and drain each FRL bowl daily. If the fault appears at
any time and worsens under load, the cylinder seals are worn and the clamp is no
longer making its rated force — this will also show as a soft crease and a
"crease didn't last" complaint from customers, so the two symptoms belong together. If
the fault appears only on heavy garments at setting 4, the supply pressure is below
the 520 kPa minimum.

## 12. Warranty and service

### 12.1 Terms

Sankosha warrants each machine on this line against defects in materials and
workmanship for **24 months from the date of commissioning**, and the steam-side
castings — heads, plates and bucks — for **60 months**. The warranty covers parts and
labour during ordinary business hours at the installed address.

Commissioning dates for the machines covered by this manual are 12 February 2018 for
the LP-580 and UP-120, and 4 November 2019 for the TT-240 and TL-260. The parts and
labour warranty on all four has expired. The steam-side casting warranty on the
TT-240 and TL-260 ran to 4 November 2024. This section is retained because it also
sets out the ongoing conditions that govern service work and the safety certification
obligation, which does not expire with the warranty.

### 12.2 Exclusions

The warranty does not cover:

- consumable items: pads, covers, felts, skins, filters, press cloths, hoses,
  strainer screens, gaskets, seal kits and lubricant;
- damage caused by steam quality — wet steam, carryover, scale or corrosion from
  untreated boiler feedwater;
- damage caused by compressed air quality outside ISO 8573-1 class 4.4.3;
- damage caused by supply voltage outside 400 V ±6%, or by phase failure;
- damage caused by operating a machine with a defeated, bypassed, disconnected or
  removed guard, interlock, two-hand control or emergency stop;
- damage caused by pressing articles excluded under 1.5;
- fair wear and tear, including cover glazing, pad compression and skin stretch;
- work carried out by a person who is not a Sankosha authorised technician;
- consequential loss, including garment damage, lost production and rework.

### 12.3 Mandatory guard and two-hand control certification

The owner must have every guard interlock, two-hand control and emergency stop on
this line tested and certified annually by a Sankosha authorised technician. The
certificate must record each device tested, the method used, the result and the
technician's authorisation number, and must be retained for five years.

This obligation is not discharged by the monthly in-house tests under 10.6. The
monthly tests are the owner's own check that the devices still work; the annual
certification is an independent verification of the safety circuit, including the
safety relay, the wiring and the measured response times.

**A machine without a current certificate is not to be operated.**

### 12.4 What voids the warranty and the certification

Any one of the following voids both the warranty and the current safety certificate
immediately:

- defeating a two-hand control by any means, including taping, tying, wedging, or
  operating one button with anything other than a hand;
- removing, bypassing or bridging a guard interlock;
- disabling an emergency stop or fitting a non-approved replacement;
- replacing a dual-channel safety relay with a general-purpose relay;
- altering the two-hand control timing window from 500 ms;
- fitting non-Sankosha pads, covers or skins that alter the closing gap;
- operating a machine after a safety device has failed a test under 10.6;
- raising the steam pressure above 620 kPa, or a head or plate temperature setpoint
  above the range given in 2.3.

### 12.5 Service and parts

Quote the model and serial number with every service call and every parts order. Have
ready the fault code, the date and time it occurred, what the machine was doing, and
whether it has occurred before. A service call booked with a code and a pattern is
usually resolved in one visit; one booked as "the shirt machine isn't working" is
usually two.

Keep the completed records in Appendices A to D with the machine. A technician
attending a finishing complaint will ask for the pad and cover change log before
anything else, because a worn cover explains more finishing complaints than every
electrical fault on this line put together.

Faults: shine, seam impression, double crease, water spotting, scorch, flattened nap, pressed-in stain, collar puckering, colour change under heat, glazing at the crease, damp garment at the hanger, cracked or melted buttons, lining pulled and rippled, and shrinkage on wool. Scorch, colour change, shrinkage and melted buttons are not recoverable; pressed-in stain rarely is.
Fault codes: SU-01 to SU-18 (LP-580), UP-01 to UP-10 (UP-120), TT-01 to TT-09 (TT-240), TL-01 to TL-09 (TL-260), each marked technician or operator; 11.5 troubleshoots the eight commonest.
Service intervals: daily and weekly by the operator, monthly and above by supervisor or technician. Monthly two-hand control, interlock, light curtain, E-stop and manual release tests; quarterly steam trap test; annual electrical test and full safety certification.
Warranty 24 months from commissioning, 60 months on steam-side castings; commissioned 12 February 2018 and 4 November 2019, all cover now expired.
Guards, two-hand controls and E-stops must be certified annually by an authorised technician; without a current certificate a machine is not to be operated. Defeating a two-hand control or interlock, or altering the 500 ms timing window, voids both warranty and certificate.

documents.text:
# TREVIL FINISHING ROOM

## Diamant SA-90 · Princess FF-300 · Spotmaster SB-40

### Combined Operating, Spotting and Maintenance Manual

**Models covered by this manual**

| Model | Machine type | Serial number | Manufactured | Installed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diamant SA-90 | Single-station steam-air cabinet finisher | DSA90-2017-0231 | 2017 | May 2017 |
| Princess FF-300 | Inflatable form finisher ("Suzy") | PFF300-2019-0884 | 2019 | October 2019 |
| Spotmaster SB-40 | Vacuum spotting board with steam gun, air gun and two chemical guns | SSB40-2016-0512 | 2016 | November 2016 |

**Installed at:** Main Street Dry Cleaners, Shop 4, 118 Hargreaves Street, Bendigo VIC 3550
**Manual revision:** Rev 3
**Revision date:** September 2020
**Supersedes:** Rev 2, March 2017

---

### Revision history

| Rev | Date | Summary of change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 09/2014 | First issue. Diamant SA series and Spotmaster SB series only. |
| 2 | 03/2017 | Added Princess FF-300 form finisher. Revised steam service data. Added fault codes FF-01 to FF-09. |
| 3 | 09/2020 | Combined the three machines into one finishing-room manual. Expanded the spotting chemistry and stain treatment tables. Added fault codes SA-13 to SA-15, FF-10 to FF-12 and SB-08 to SB-11. Revised local exhaust ventilation figures at the spotting board. Added Appendix D. |

---

## 1. Front matter

### 1.1 Scope of this manual

This manual covers the three Trevil finishing machines supplied as a finishing
line: the Diamant SA-90 steam-air cabinet finisher, the Princess FF-300 form
finisher, and the Spotmaster SB-40 spotting board. The three machines are
described in one manual because they share a steam supply, a compressed air
supply and an operator, and because a garment normally passes through the
spotting board before it reaches either finisher.

The manual is written for three readers:

- the **operator**, who loads and runs the machines and does the daily and
  weekly maintenance;
- the **spotter**, who works at the SB-40 and makes decisions about chemistry
  and about which garments must not be treated;
- the **technician**, who holds the relevant electrical, plumbing or mechanical
  licence and does the work marked TECHNICIAN in this manual.

The manual does not teach finishing and it does not teach garment
identification. It assumes the reader is a competent presser or spotter. It
tells you what each machine does, what it needs from the building, what to set,
what to check, and what to do when it stops.

Keep this manual in the finishing room, not in the office. If a machine is
sold, relocated or transferred, this manual and the commissioning record in
Appendix A go with it.

Nothing in this manual overrides a legal duty imposed on the occupier of the
premises. Where a requirement of this manual conflicts with a requirement of a
regulator, the regulator's requirement applies.

### 1.2 How to use this manual

- **If you are new to the finishing room**, read Section 2 (Safety) in full
  before you touch any of the three machines. Then read the description section
  for the machine you have been put on: Section 5 for the SA-90, Section 6 for
  the FF-300, Section 7 for the SB-40.
- **If you are setting a programme**, the parameter list and the programme table
  for the SA-90 are at 5.5 and 5.6, and for the FF-300 at 6.5 and 6.6. Print the
  programme table and keep it at the machine.
- **If you are spotting**, Section 7 is the whole of your reference. The stain
  treatment table is at 7.6. Read 7.8 (fibre cautions) and 7.9 (when not to
  spot) before you use the table, not after.
- **If a machine has stopped and is showing a code**, go straight to Section 9.
  Find the code. The table tells you whether an operator may clear it or whether
  a technician is required. If the table says technician, stop and call one.
- **If you are ordering parts**, use Section 10 and quote the serial number of
  the machine with every order.
- **If a contractor is quoting service work**, Section 8 sets out the intervals
  and Section 11 sets out what voids warranty.

Cross-references are written as "see 7.6" meaning sub-section 7.6. Fault codes
are always written in the form SA-04, FF-03 or SB-05 and mean the same thing
wherever they appear in this manual. The two-letter prefix identifies the
machine: SA is the Diamant SA-90, FF is the Princess FF-300, SB is the
Spotmaster SB-40.

### 1.3 Symbols used in this manual

| Symbol word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DANGER** | A hazard that will cause death or serious injury if the instruction is not followed. |
| **WARNING** | A hazard that may cause death or serious injury if the instruction is not followed. |
| **CAUTION** | A hazard that may cause minor injury, or that will damage the machine or the garment. |
| **NOTE** | Information that affects the result of the work but is not a hazard. |
| **TECHNICIAN** | The task must be done by a person holding the relevant trade licence or the manufacturer's service authorisation. An operator must not attempt it. |
| **GARMENT RISK** | The instruction exists to prevent damage to the customer's garment, not to the machine. Damage of this kind is usually not recoverable. |

### 1.4 Machine identification

Each machine carries a data plate:

- **SA-90** — right-hand side panel, 1,450 mm above floor level, beside the
  electrical isolator. Carries model, serial number, year of manufacture, supply
  voltage, full load current, total connected load, steam design pressure and
  maximum air temperature.
- **FF-300** — rear panel above the steam inlet, 1,300 mm above floor level.
  Carries the same data plus the maximum form inflation pressure.
- **SB-40** — underside of the board frame at the left-hand front leg. Carries
  model, serial number, year of manufacture, supply voltage, vacuum motor rating
  and the maximum regulated pressure at the chemical guns.

Do not paint over, cover or remove a data plate. If a plate becomes unreadable,
order a replacement quoting the serial number recorded at the head of this
manual.

### 1.5 Intended use

The SA-90 and the FF-300 are intended to finish clean, dry or nearly dry textile
garments by the controlled application of saturated steam followed by heated air
and a cooling airflow. The SB-40 is intended for the localised removal of stains
from textile garments using steam, compressed air, vacuum extraction and the
proprietary spotting chemistry listed at 7.4.

None of the three machines may be used:

- on a garment that is wet with solvent, or that has come directly out of a dry
  cleaning machine without completing its drying and deodorising cycle;
- on a garment contaminated with flammable liquid, oxidiser, paint solvent,
  adhesive or unidentified chemical residue;
- to dry a garment that has been washed and not extracted;
- as a bench, a shelf, or a place to hang finished work.

The SB-40 must not be used with any chemistry other than that listed at 7.4, or
with any product for which the Safety Data Sheet is not held on site.

### 1.6 Residual risks

Even when all three machines are used as intended and all guards are fitted, the
following risks remain and must be managed by the occupier:

- burns from steam, condensate and hot metal at all three machines;
- inhalation of steam and of chemical mist at the spotting board;
- eye injury from the air gun, from the chemical guns, and from splashback off
  the board;
- skin contact with acidic, alkaline and solvent spotting agents;
- fire risk from volatile dry-side spotting agents, in particular amyl acetate;
- slips on a wet floor around the spotting board;
- manual handling of heavy coats onto the SA-90 hanger and of the FF-300 form
  cover during replacement;
- electrical risk from equipment operated in a wet area.

---

## 2. Safety

### 2.1 General

**WARNING.** The finishing room contains steam at up to 690 kPa, surfaces above
150 °C, compressed air at 620 kPa and chemicals that burn skin and eyes. Three
of the four will injure a person without making any noise first. Do not work in
the finishing room without the personal protective equipment listed at 2.6.

Only trained personnel may operate these machines. Training must be recorded and
must cover, as a minimum: the emergency stop locations, the steam isolation
valve locations, the meaning of every fault code for the machine the person will
operate, the PPE requirements, and the location of the eyewash and the Safety
Data Sheets.

### 2.2 Steam and hot surfaces

Steam supplied to these machines is saturated steam at up to 690 kPa. At 550 kPa
the saturation temperature is approximately 160 °C. Steam escaping from a failed
hose or a cracked fitting is invisible for the first 100 mm to 200 mm of its
path and will remove skin at any distance at which it can still be heard.

**DANGER.** Never search for a steam leak with your hand. Use a board, a broom
handle or a sheet of paper held at arm's length and watch for the paper to be
pushed, wetted or cut.

Hot surfaces on these machines include:

- the SA-90 steam manifold, cabinet floor tray and the lower 400 mm of the
  cabinet rear wall;
- the SA-90 hot air duct and heater housing, which remain above 60 °C for up to
  20 minutes after the last cycle;
- the FF-300 steam ring, blower housing and heater housing;
- the SB-40 steam gun body, hose and nozzle, at all times while the steam
  isolation valve is open;
- all condensate pipework and steam traps at all three machines.

**WARNING.** The SB-40 steam gun nozzle reaches approximately 155 °C in normal
use. Do not rest it on the board cover. Return it to its holder after every
application. A gun left lying on the board will scorch the cover and will burn
the next hand that reaches for the board.

Do not open the SA-90 cabinet during the steam phase. Do not stand directly in
front of the FF-300 form during the pre-steam phase; steam vents forward through
the garment opening.

### 2.3 Chemical hazards at the spotting board

The spotting board is the most hazardous position in the finishing room. The
chemistry set listed at 7.4 includes strong alkalis, strong acids, an oxidising
bleach, a reducing agent, a volatile ester and hydrocarbon solvent.

**WARNING.** The following combinations must never be made on the board, in a
bottle, in the drip tray or in a rinse pot:

- oxygen bleach with any acid formula, including tannin formula and rust
  remover — releases oxygen violently and may release chlorine-like irritants
  where residues of other products are present;
- rust remover with any alkaline product — exothermic, and generates a corrosive
  aerosol at the fabric surface;
- amyl acetate with any oxidiser;
- any two products from different bottles decanted into one container "to save a
  step".

Flush the board with steam and vacuum it dry between an acid-side and an
alkali-side treatment. This is not optional and it is not a courtesy to the next
garment; it is how the operator avoids generating a reaction under their own
face.

**WARNING — amyl acetate.** Amyl acetate (TVC-05) is a flammable liquid with a
flash point of approximately 25 °C and a strong pear-drop odour. It must be:

- used only under the local exhaust hood, with the hood running;
- kept in its original 250 mL supplier bottle with the cap closed between uses;
- kept away from the steam gun, the heater of any nearby machine, and any
  ignition source;
- never decanted into a chemical gun bottle;
- never used in a quantity greater than is needed to wet the stain.

The volatile dry-side solvent (TVC-09) is a hydrocarbon with a flash point above
62 °C. It is less hazardous than amyl acetate but must still be used under
exhaust and kept closed.

### 2.4 Ventilation and local exhaust at the spotting board

The SB-40 is fitted with a rear-draught local exhaust hood connected to a
dedicated extraction fan discharging to atmosphere. The hood must achieve a face
velocity of not less than 0.5 m/s measured at the centre of the hood opening,
corresponding to approximately 850 m³/h at this hood size.

**DANGER.** Do not use the chemical guns, amyl acetate or the dry-side solvent
when the extraction fan is not running. There is no safe way to do this for
"just one spot".

The extraction fan must be interlocked with, or started before, the vacuum
blower. A green lamp on the SB-40 control box indicates airflow proved by the
differential pressure switch across the hood. If the lamp is out, the machine
will raise SB-11; stop chemical work and report it.

Face velocity must be measured and recorded quarterly (see 8.5). General
finishing room ventilation must provide not less than 8 air changes per hour
with the finishing room doors closed. Make-up air must be provided; extraction
without make-up air will pull the hood short. Exhaust discharge must not be
located where it can re-enter the building through a door, a window or an air
intake.

The SB-40 hood must **not** be joined into a common duct with the finisher
vents. A common duct allows the finishers' higher-flow branch to short-circuit
the hood.

### 2.5 Compressed air and eye injury

The SB-40 air gun and the SA-90 sleeve expander circuit are supplied with
compressed air at 620 kPa. Compressed air at this pressure will:

- drive lint, fibre, dried chemistry and rust particles into an unprotected eye
  at a speed that no blink reflex will beat;
- inject air under the skin through a cut or a hangnail;
- atomise whatever is lying on the board into a breathable mist.

**DANGER.** Never direct the air gun at a person, at your own hand, or at your
own clothing. Never use the air gun to clean yourself down. Never use it to
sweep the floor or the bench.

**WARNING.** Eye protection is mandatory whenever the air gun or either chemical
gun is used. This applies to the operator and to anyone within 2 m of the board.

### 2.6 Personal protective equipment

| Task | Eye protection | Hand protection | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loading and running SA-90 | Not required | Not required; heat-resistant glove if handling the tray | Closed footwear |
| Loading and running FF-300 | Not required | Not required | Closed footwear |
| Spotting, wet side (SB-40) | Safety glasses with side shields, minimum | Nitrile gloves, minimum 0.11 mm | Chemical-resistant apron |
| Spotting, dry side or bleaching | Chemical splash goggles | Nitrile gloves, minimum 0.11 mm | Apron; hood running |
| Decanting chemistry | Chemical splash goggles | Nitrile gloves, minimum 0.11 mm | Apron; hood running; face shield if decanting more than 1 L |
| Steam trap testing, hot work | Safety glasses | Heat-resistant gauntlet | Long sleeves |
| Cleaning vacuum filter | Safety glasses | Nitrile gloves | P2 disposable respirator |
| Changing FF-300 form cover | Not required | Not required | Two people for the lift |

Nitrile gloves are the standard glove for the whole chemistry set at 7.4. Do not
substitute latex; latex is permeated quickly by amyl acetate and by the dry-side
solvent. Change gloves as soon as chemical reaches the inside.

### 2.7 Electrical safety near water

The SB-40 sits in a wet area. The board is wetted, the floor around it is
wetted, and the operator's hands are wet.

**DANGER.** The SB-40 supply must be protected by a residual current device of
30 mA rating. Test the RCD monthly using its own test button and record the
result in the weekly log sheet at Appendix B.

- Do not hose or flood-wash the floor while any machine is energised.
- Do not use a damaged flexible lead. Report and tag it out.
- Do not run extension leads across the finishing room floor.
- Keep the SB-40 control box lid closed and latched. It is rated IP54 with the
  lid closed and IP00 with it open.
- Steam and water must never be directed at the control box, at the lamp
  transformer or at the vacuum motor.

**TECHNICIAN.** Any work inside a control enclosure, any change to the supply,
and any RCD replacement is licensed electrical work.

### 2.8 Emergency stop

Each machine has an emergency stop:

- **SA-90** — red mushroom head, front upright, right-hand side, 1,050 mm above
  floor level.
- **FF-300** — red mushroom head, control pedestal front face; and a second
  mushroom head on the rear panel beside the steam inlet.
- **SB-40** — red mushroom head, front rail below the board, left of the vacuum
  pedal.

Pressing an emergency stop de-energises the heaters, the fan or blower, the
tension and inflation drives, and closes the steam solenoid on that machine.
It does not isolate the incoming electrical supply, and it does not isolate the
steam supply upstream of the solenoid. To make a machine safe for maintenance,
use the lock-out procedure at 8.2.

Emergency stops must be tested weekly (see 8.3 to 8.5). A machine whose
emergency stop does not stop the machine must be tagged out of service
immediately.

### 2.9 First aid — steam or contact burn

1. Move the person away from the source. Do not go back for the machine.
2. Cool the burn under cool running water for **20 minutes**. Do not use ice,
   iced water, butter, oil, toothpaste or any cream.
3. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the burn while cooling, unless
   fabric is stuck to the skin. Do not pull fabric off a burn.
4. Cover loosely with cling film laid along the limb, or a clean non-fluffy
   cloth. Do not wrap tightly and do not wrap circumferentially.
5. Keep the person warm elsewhere on the body; 20 minutes of cooling will chill
   them.
6. Seek medical attention for any burn that is larger than a 20-cent coin, any
   burn to the face, hands, feet, groin or across a joint, any burn that is
   white, brown or leathery, and any burn to a young or an older worker.
7. Record the incident. A steam burn that needed more than a plaster is a
   notifiable-incident question; the occupier decides, not the injured person.

### 2.10 First aid — chemical splash

**To the eye:**

1. Go to the eyewash immediately. Do not finish the garment first.
2. Hold the eyelids open and flush with gentle running water for at least
   **20 minutes**, longer for alkali. Roll the eye to flush under the lids.
3. Remove contact lenses after the first minute of flushing if they have not
   already washed out.
4. Seek medical attention for every chemical eye splash without exception. Take
   the Safety Data Sheet with you.

**To the skin:**

1. Flush with running water for at least 15 minutes.
2. Remove contaminated clothing while flushing.
3. Do not attempt to neutralise an acid with an alkali or an alkali with an acid
   on skin. The heat of reaction makes the injury worse.
4. Seek medical attention for any blistering, any burn to the face, or any
   contact with rust remover or with oxygen bleach at working strength.

**Swallowed:**

1. Do not induce vomiting.
2. Rinse the mouth with water. Give water to drink if the person is conscious.
3. Ring the Poisons Information Centre on **13 11 26** and follow their
   direction. Have the Safety Data Sheet in your hand when you ring.

**Inhaled:**

1. Move the person to fresh air away from the board.
2. If breathing is difficult, ring 000.
3. Do not send the person back to the board for the rest of the shift.

An eyewash station and a first aid kit must be within 10 seconds' unobstructed
travel of the SB-40. The eyewash must be flushed weekly and the flush recorded.

---

## 3. Services required

### 3.1 Steam

All three machines take saturated steam from the plant boiler through a common
DN32 header, dropped to each machine through an isolation valve, a strainer and
a separator. Each machine has its own trap set discharging to the common DN25
condensate return.

Steam must be dry saturated. Wet steam will spot a garment at the SA-90 and will
spit water out of the SB-40 gun onto the exact area being spotted. If the steam
is wet, the cause is upstream: a flooded main, a failed separator, a boiler
carrying over, or a trap that has failed closed.

**NOTE.** Steam supply pressure at the header must not fall below 400 kPa while
two machines are calling for steam at once. Below 400 kPa the SA-90 will not
produce a full steam phase and will eventually log SA-01.

### 3.2 Condensate

Each machine has a float-thermostatic trap sized for its own load. The trap set
comprises isolation valve, strainer, trap, sight check and non-return valve into
the common return. The return line falls at not less than 1:100 back to the feed
tank.

Do not manifold two traps into one branch without a non-return valve on each.
The SB-40 trap is much smaller than the other two and will be back-pressured by
the SA-90 if this is done, which puts water in the gun.

### 3.3 Compressed air

Compressed air is taken from the plant receiver through a DN15 branch to a
filter-regulator-lubricator set at each machine. The SB-40 air gun branch must
be taken from the **filtered, unlubricated** leg. Oil carried through to the air
gun will be blown into the garment.

Air must be dry to a pressure dew point of at least 3 °C at line pressure. Water
in the SB-40 air gun will make a ring on every garment it touches.

### 3.4 Vacuum

Vacuum at the SB-40 is generated by the machine's own integral side-channel
blower. No external vacuum service is required. The blower exhausts through the
lint screen and the filter element into the machine base and then to the local
exhaust duct.

### 3.5 Electrical

Each machine has its own isolator within 2 m and in line of sight. The SA-90 and
FF-300 are three-phase; the SB-40 is single-phase and must be RCD-protected as
required by 2.7.

**TECHNICIAN.** Phase rotation matters for the SA-90 fan and the FF-300 blower.
Reversed rotation gives reduced airflow, poor finishing, and eventually a heater
over-temperature trip. Check rotation at every reconnection.

### 3.6 Exhaust ventilation

| Point | Duct | Design flow | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| SB-40 local exhaust hood | 200 mm | 850 m³/h | Face velocity ≥ 0.5 m/s. Discharge to atmosphere. Dedicated fan. |
| SA-90 cabinet vent spigot | 160 mm | 400 m³/h | Removes cabinet steam at door open. May join a common finishing extract. |
| FF-300 canopy | 160 mm | 300 m³/h | Optional but strongly recommended; without it the room humidity rises. |
| Finishing room general | — | 8 air changes/h | Make-up air must be provided; extraction without make-up air will pull the SB-40 hood short. |

**NOTE.** The line total for steam assumes the three machines are not all in

---

## 5. Diamant SA-90 steam-air finisher

### 5.1 Description

The Diamant SA-90 is a single-station enclosed cabinet finisher. A garment is
hung on a powered hanger inside a steel cabinet, tensioned from the hem, and
subjected in sequence to a saturated steam phase, a hot air phase and a cool air
phase. The purpose of the machine is to relax the fibre, remove creases set by
handling and by the dry cleaning machine, restore the garment's shape, and dry
and set it in that shape before it is unloaded.

The cabinet is a welded steel enclosure with a stainless steel liner, insulated
on all four walls and the roof with 25 mm mineral wool. The front is a
counterweighted door with a laminated glass panel. The floor of the cabinet is a
sloped stainless tray draining to the condensate tundish through a 40 mm trap.

The steam manifold sits behind a perforated diffuser plate on the rear wall.
Twelve nozzles distribute steam across the full working height. A separator and
a strainer upstream of the solenoid keep condensate out of the manifold.

The hot air battery sits above the cabinet roof. The 0.75 kW centrifugal fan
draws room air through a washable inlet filter, over the 9.8 kW heater bank, and
delivers it down the rear plenum and out through the same diffuser plate. The
two heater stages are switched independently by the controller so that the
machine can hold low air temperatures for delicate work without cycling the full
bank.

The controller is a 24-programme unit with a four-line display and a keypad.
Programmes 1 to 12 are factory-set and can be edited but not deleted;
programmes 13 to 24 are free.

### 5.2 The tensioning system

The hanger is fixed. Tension is applied downwards from a hem clamp assembly that
runs on a linear rail at the bottom of the cabinet. A geared 24 V DC motor drives
the clamp down against a load cell until the programmed tension force is
reached, then holds it under closed-loop control for the whole cycle.

Tension is programmed as a percentage of full scale. The relationship is linear:

| Setting | Force |
|---|---|
| 0% | 120 N |
| 25% | 190 N |
| 50% | 260 N |
| 55% | 274 N |
| 75% | 330 N |
| 100% | 400 N |

Tension does what a presser's hands do on a form: it takes out the horizontal
wrinkling that steam alone will not remove, and it holds the length of the
garment while the fibre is plastic. Too little tension and the garment comes out
with a soft, unfinished body. Too much and you will stretch the hem, mark the
fabric at the clamp, and on knitwear you will change the garment's size.

**GARMENT RISK.** Do not use tension above 40% on knitwear, above 35% on silk,
or above 30% on any garment with elastane in the ground weave. These fabrics do
not recover.

The clamp pads are silicone-faced, part TV-SA-4210. Replace them when the
silicone glazes; a glazed pad slips and then grips suddenly, which is how hems
get marked.

### 5.3 Shoulder and sleeve expanders

The **shoulder expanders** are two pivoting plates carried on the hanger yoke.
They travel outward from the centre by 0 to 60 mm per side, driven by a small
pneumatic cylinder through a scissor linkage. Their job is to fill the shoulder
of a jacket or coat so that the steam does not set a hollow at the shoulder
point. Set the travel so that the shoulder seam of the garment sits flat and the
sleeve head is round; do not set it so far that the shoulder seam is pulled
outboard of the garment's own shoulder line.

The **sleeve expanders** are two inflatable bladders that hang inside the sleeves
from the yoke. They are inflated from the compressed air supply through an
independent regulator, 0.5 to 2.5 bar. They fill the sleeve so that the sleeve is
finished round rather than pressed flat with a crease down each side.

Sleeve expander bladders are part TV-SA-1120 and are supplied as a pair. They
are a consumable. Expect 18 to 30 months in a plant running 1,000 garments a
week. A bladder that will not hold pressure will show as a slow air leak and, in
time, as fault SA-03 during the inflation step.

**NOTE.** Sleeve expanders are not used on shirts, on knitwear or on any
sleeveless garment. Set P8 to 0 for those programmes so that the bladders are
not cycled unnecessarily.

### 5.4 The finishing cycle

The SA-90 cycle has five phases and always runs in this order:

1. **Load and tension.** The operator hangs the garment, closes the door and
   presses start. The hem clamp descends and takes up to the programmed force.
   The shoulder and sleeve expanders deploy. Typical duration 6 to 10 s.
2. **Steam.** The steam solenoid opens for the programmed steam time. Saturated
   steam at 550 kPa enters through the diffuser. The fan runs at 30% during this
   phase to distribute steam without cooling it. The purpose is to raise the
   fibre above its glass transition temperature and let internal stresses relax.
3. **Soak.** The steam solenoid closes and the garment is held, still tensioned,
   with no airflow. This lets the moisture equalise through the thickness of the
   cloth instead of sitting on the face. Typical 3 to 6 s. Wool and heavy coating
   need more soak; thin synthetics need almost none.
4. **Hot air.** The heater bank energises and the fan goes to the programmed
   speed. Heated air at the programmed temperature dries the garment while it is
   still under tension. This is the phase that sets the shape.
5. **Cool.** The heaters de-energise and the fan continues at full speed with
   ambient air. The garment must come down through its glass transition
   temperature while still tensioned, or the shape set in phase 4 will relax as
   soon as the tension is released. Skipping the cool phase is the single most
   common cause of a garment that looks finished at the machine and looks
   unfinished on the rail 20 minutes later.

The clamp releases and the expanders retract at the end of the cool phase. The
door may then be opened.

### 5.5 Parameter list

| Ref | Parameter | Range | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Steam time | 0–45 s | 12 s | The main variable. More steam relaxes more, and wets more. |
| P2 | Soak time | 0–20 s | 4 s | Increase for thick or felted cloth. |
| P3 | Air temperature | 45–130 °C | 85 °C | Setpoint at the plenum sensor, not at the garment. |
| P4 | Hot air time | 10–180 s | 60 s | Must be long enough to dry, not longer. |
| P5 | Cool time | 0–60 s | 20 s | Never set below 10 s on wool or on any tailored garment. |
| P6 | Tension | 0–100% | 55% | See the force table at 5.2. |
| P7 | Shoulder expander travel | 0–60 mm | 30 mm | Per side. |
| P8 | Sleeve expander pressure | 0–2.5 bar | 1.4 bar | 0 disables the bladders. |
| P9 | Steam pulses | 1–3 | 1 | Splits P1 into equal pulses with 2 s gaps. Use on heavy coating. |
| P10 | Fan speed, hot air phase | 40–100% | 80% | Reduce for lightweight fabrics that lift and flap. |
| P11 | Fan speed, cool phase | 60–100% | 100% | Rarely changed. |
| P12 | Steam pressure trip delay | 2–15 s | 5 s | Time below 400 kPa before SA-01 is raised. |
| P13 | Cycle timeout | 120–300 s | 240 s | Total cycle limit before SA-10. |
| P14 | Door interlock mode | 0 or 1 | 1 | 1 = cycle aborts on door open. Do not set 0. |

**TECHNICIAN.** P12, P13 and P14 are under the service menu and require the
service code. P14 must not be changed. A machine found with P14 set to 0 is out
of compliance with its own guarding and must be tagged out until corrected.

Tension in per cent of full scale. Sleeve pressure in bar.

| 01 | Wool suit jacket | 14 | 6 | 95 | 65 | 25 | 55% | 35 mm | 1.6 |

**Notes on individual programmes**

- **01 Wool suit jacket.** The reference programme. If a jacket needs more than
  P1 = 18 s to relax, it is either badly creased from the cleaning machine or it
  has been overdried. Fix the cause upstream rather than steaming harder.
- **02 Wool trousers.** Higher tension than the jacket because the leg must be
  held straight. Run the trousers on the finisher only to relax the leg; the
  crease is put in on the legger, not here.
- **03 Polyester blend suit.** Lower temperature than wool. Polyester holds a
  heat-set crease that will not come out on this machine, so do not increase P3
  in the hope of removing one.
- **04 Cotton chinos.** Cotton needs heat and time, not extra steam. If the
  crease will not hold, the answer is a longer cool phase, not a hotter one.
- **05 Silk blouse.** Low tension, low temperature, short everything. Watch for
  water spotting; if the first garment of the day spots, the steam line is wet
  and needs to be blown through before the shift starts.
- **06 Knitwear.** The soak time is deliberately longer than the steam time. The
  point is to let the moisture through the yarn without loading the surface.
  Tension must stay low or the garment will come off longer than it went on.
- **07 Overcoat.** Use P9 = 2 (two steam pulses) on heavy melton or on a coat
  that has been hanging pressed flat in the store. The gap between pulses lets
  the first charge penetrate before the second arrives.
- **08 Uniform.** Most uniform cloth is a poly/wool blend with a permanent
  finish. Keep P3 at 80 °C; above about 95 °C the finish glazes at the shoulder.
- **09 Workwear.** The most tolerant programme in the list. Cotton drill takes
  heat, time and tension, and the finish wanted is flat rather than round.
- **10 Down jacket.** The long air time is drying, not finishing. Down that is
  not fully dry will clump and smell within a day. Do not tension a down jacket;
  20% is enough to keep it hanging straight.
- **11 Raincoat.** Coated and laminated fabrics can delaminate above 60 °C. If
  the garment carries no fibre content label, do not run it on this machine.
- **12 Lined skirt.** Clamp the shell only. A skirt lining clamped with the shell
  will finish with a drag line at the hem.

### 5.7 Loading technique

1. Check the garment against the spotter's ticket. A garment that has come back
   from the SB-40 with an unresolved stain must not be finished until the
   decision at 7.9 has been made and recorded; heat will set the stain.
2. Empty every pocket. A pen left in a breast pocket will burst.
3. Do up the top button or the top hook only. Buttoning a jacket all the way
   will set a drag line from the button stand.
4. Hang the garment square on the hanger. The centre back seam must sit on the
   centre of the yoke. A garment hung 20 mm off centre will finish with one
   shoulder higher than the other and no amount of steam will fix it afterwards.
5. Dress the collar down flat and turn the lapels to their natural roll line.
6. Feed the sleeve expanders into the sleeves before you close the door. Do not
   force a bladder into a narrow sleeve; deflate it, feed it, then inflate.
7. Bring the hem clamp up by hand to the hem, centre it, and let the machine take
   up the tension. Do not clamp a lining separately from the shell.
8. Close the door fully. The interlock must click.
9. Select the programme and press start. Watch the first 5 s. If the tension
   overshoots or the garment shifts, stop and reload.
10. Unload as soon as the cycle finishes. A garment left standing in a warm
    cabinet picks up moisture from the tray as the cabinet cools.

### 5.8 Over-finishing — what it looks like

Over-finishing is too much steam, too much heat, too much time, or too much
tension. It shows as:

- **Shine or glazing** on the face of the cloth, especially at the shoulder,
  elbow, seat and any point where a seam allowance lies underneath. On dark
  worsted this is visible from three metres and it is usually permanent.
- **Seam impressions** — the outline of the seam allowance or the pocket bag
  printed through onto the face.
- **Flattened nap** on velvet, moleskin, corduroy or brushed wool.
- **Stretched hems and cuffs**, and on knitwear a garment that is measurably
  longer than it was.
- **Yellowing** on white silk and on wool, from excess heat.
- **Puckered seams** where the shell and the interlining have shrunk at
  different rates.
- **A garment that is damp in the lining and dry on the face**, because the air
  time was increased to force a result that the steam time caused.

The correction is nearly always to reduce P1 and P3 together, not one of them.

### 5.9 Under-finishing — what it looks like

- **Residual body wrinkling** through the back and the sleeve, particularly the
  horizontal wrinkling from the cleaning machine drum.
- **A collapsed shoulder line** or a sleeve head that is not round.
- **Creases that come back** within 20 minutes on the rail. This is a cool-phase
  failure, not a steam failure. Increase P5 before you touch anything else.
- **Damp garments**, which then mark on the conveyor and go out smelling stale.
- **A soft, limp body** on a tailored garment, meaning tension was too low.

If a garment comes out under-finished, do not simply run it again on the same
programme. Two identical inadequate cycles put twice the moisture into the
garment for the same result. Change the programme.

## 6. Princess FF-300 form finisher

### 6.1 Description

The Princess FF-300 is a form finisher, commonly called a Suzy. The garment is
dressed onto a fabric-covered form which is then inflated with heated air from
inside. Where the SA-90 blows air past a garment hanging in a cabinet, the
FF-300 blows air through the garment from the inside out, so the garment is
finished against its own tension rather than against a press.

The machine consists of a steel pedestal, a 1.5 kW centrifugal blower, a 6.0 kW
two-stage heater battery, a steam ring at the base of the form, an inflatable
form on an adjustable shoulder yoke, two sleeve bladders, a collar clamp, and a
pair of hem clamps on a vertically adjustable rail. The control pedestal carries
the display, keypad, foot pedal and the front emergency stop.

Air path: the blower draws room air through a washable filter, passes it over
the heater battery, and delivers it into the base of the form. The form fabric
is permeable; air passes through the form, through the garment, and out. Steam
is injected into the same plenum during the pre-steam phase so that the garment
is steamed from the inside before the hot air starts.

### 6.2 The form

The form is a shaped, air-permeable fabric bag on a wire and plate frame. The
standard cover is TV-FF-1000; a jacket-profile cover with a firmer shoulder and
a longer body is TV-FF-1001. The cover is a consumable and is the single part
that most affects finish quality.

Form inflation pressure is programmed in kilopascals, 0.8 to 4.5 kPa, with a
relief valve set at 5.0 kPa. Inflation is what holds the garment out. Too little
and the garment is finished slack, with wrinkling left in the body. Too much and
the garment is stretched — on a shirt the buttons gape and the button stand
distorts; on a jacket the front edges bow outwards and will not sit closed
afterwards.

Cover condition matters. A cover that has hardened, glazed or gone stiff at the
shoulder will no longer pass air evenly and will print its own seams onto the
inside of a light garment. Replace the cover on condition (see 8.7), typically
every 9 to 15 months at 1,000 garments a week.

### 6.3 Clamping and tensioning

- **Hem clamps.** Two spring-loaded clamps on a vertical rail, adjustable from
  620 mm to 840 mm below the shoulder plate. They pull the garment down against
  the inflation. Programmed as a percentage, F7; 100% is approximately 90 N per
  clamp.
- **Collar clamp.** A pivoting bar that closes over the collar band and holds the
  neck down onto the shoulder yoke. Used on shirts and on anything with a stand
  collar. Not used on a jacket with a rolled collar.
- **Shoulder plates.** Adjustable 380 mm to 520 mm across. Set to the garment's
  own shoulder width, measured seam to seam. This is the most important single
  setting on the machine.
- **Sleeve bladders.** Inflated separately, 0.5 to 3.0 kPa, part TV-FF-1010.

### 6.4 Jacket versus shirt on the form

They are not the same job and the settings are not close to each other.

A **shirt** is a single layer of woven cotton or blend with no interlining except
in the collar and cuffs. It wants high airflow, moderate inflation, high
temperature and a short cycle. The collar clamp is on. The hem clamps are set
firm so the shirt tail is pulled taut. The finish you are after is flat and dry;
a shirt off the form still needs its collar, cuffs and front placket done on the
shirt unit or a press.

A **jacket** is a built garment: shell, interlining, canvas or fusible, and a
lining that is cut to a different length from the shell on purpose. It wants
moderate airflow, low inflation, lower temperature and a longer cycle with a
proper cool phase. The collar clamp is off. The hem clamps are set light, because
a jacket hem pulled hard will drag the lining down and break the lining's ease
pleat. The finish you are after is round and soft, with the roll line of the
lapel preserved.

If you run a jacket on a shirt programme you will get a flat, over-inflated
jacket with bowed fronts and flattened lapels. If you run a shirt on a jacket
programme you will get a damp shirt.

### 6.5 Parameter list

| Ref | Parameter | Range | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | Form inflation pressure | 0.8–4.5 kPa | 2.2 kPa | The main shape control. |
| F2 | Pre-steam time | 0–20 s | 6 s | Steam into the plenum, blower at 25%. |
| F3 | Steam/air overlap | 0–15 s | 4 s | Steam continues as the heaters come on. |
| F4 | Air temperature | 40–120 °C | 75 °C | Plenum setpoint. |
| F5 | Hot air time | 10–120 s | 45 s | Drying and setting. |
| F6 | Cool time | 0–45 s | 15 s | Ambient air, form still inflated. |
| F7 | Hem clamp tension | 0–100% | 50% | 100% is approximately 90 N per clamp. |
| F8 | Sleeve inflation | 0–3.0 kPa | 1.6 kPa | 0 disables the bladders. |
| F9 | Collar clamp | On / Off | On | Off for jackets and rolled collars. |
| F10 | Shoulder plate width | 380–520 mm | 440 mm | Set to the garment, not to the programme. |
| F11 | Blower speed, hot air | 50–100% | 90% | Reduce for fine and open-weave fabrics. |
| F12 | Cycle timeout | 90–240 s | 180 s | Total cycle limit before FF-09. |

| 10 | Tunic / uniform top | 2.4 | 5 | 85 | 45 | 15 | 55% | 1.6 | On |

### 6.7 Avoiding seam ripple and shoulder distortion

**Seam ripple** is a wave along a seam, most often the side seam, the armhole or
the shoulder seam of a shirt. It is caused by the two sides of the seam being
held at different tensions while the fibre is plastic. On the FF-300 the causes,
in the order you should check them, are:

1. **Inflation too high for the garment.** The seam thread does not stretch as
   much as the cloth. Reduce F1 by 0.4 kPa and run again.
2. **Hem clamps not level.** If one clamp is set 15 mm lower than the other, one
   side seam carries the load. Level the clamps.
3. **Garment dressed off-centre**, so one shoulder is over the plate edge.
4. **Shoulder plates set wider than the garment**, stretching the shoulder seam
   across the plate ends.
5. **Cool time too short.** The seam relaxes unevenly once released.
6. **A worn form cover** with a hardened patch that does not pass air.

**Shoulder distortion** is a shoulder line that comes out square when it should
be sloped, or a divot at the shoulder point. Causes:

- shoulder plates too wide — the most common cause by a long way. Measure the
  garment shoulder seam to seam and set F10 to that figure, not to the last
  garment's figure;
- shoulder plates too narrow, giving a collapsed, rounded shoulder;
- collar clamp engaged on a garment with a rolled collar, which pulls the neck
  down and lifts the shoulder points;
- inflation too high with a light garment, which balloons the shoulder.

**NOTE.** If a garment comes off with both seam ripple and a distorted shoulder,
the cause is almost always the shoulder plate width. Fix that first and re-run.
