documents.title: SOP 01 — counter intake — Existing stains and their likely class, How to raise it, How it is completed
documents.background: How we take a garment in at both sites. Version 4, effective 1 March 2026. This is the procedure the "Tagging garments the Main Street way" training course was written from.
documents.text:
### 5.5 Existing stains and their likely class

Record where it is, how big it is, what colour it is, and what class you think it is. You are not being asked to be certain. You are being asked to say what you saw, so that Peter knows what he is looking at before he starts and so that the record shows the mark was there on the way in.

| Class | What it looks like | How to write it |
|---|---|---|
| Tannin / water-based | Tea, coffee, wine, fruit juice — brown to pink, edges usually defined | "Tannin-type mark, front right at waist, approx 30 mm" |
| Oil-based | Grease, make-up, salad oil, engine oil — darker than the fabric, no ring, feels slightly slick | "Oily mark, left lapel, approx 20 mm" |
| Protein | Blood, milk, egg, perspiration — stiff to the touch, dulls and sets with heat | "Protein-type mark, inside collar, approx 15 mm" |
| Dye | Ink, grass, some cosmetics, transferred dye — strongly coloured, sharp edge | "Blue ink, inside right cuff, approx 15 mm" |
| Invisible / aged | Sugar, soft drink, white wine, perspiration — invisible now, browns after heat | "Suspected invisible sugar staining, front skirt panel" |
| Combination | Most food marks — an oily component and a water-based one | "Food mark, front, approx 25 mm, oily and tannin" |
| Unknown | You genuinely cannot tell | "Stiffened area lower back, approx 150 mm across, origin unknown" |

The invisible class is the one that catches people. A clear drink spilled at a wedding leaves nothing to see. Six months later, after the heat of a press, it is a brown patch, and the customer is certain we made it. Whenever a garment has been to a function and has been sitting since, ask, and write the answer down:

> *"Has it had a drink on it at any point? It doesn't have to show — sugar goes brown when it's heated, so it's better if I note it now."*

**Never promise removal of any mark. Ever.** Not "we'll get that out", not "that'll come out fine", not a confident nod. What you say is:

> *"I'll have a go at that one, but I can't promise it — it's been in a while."*

And then write on the docket what you told the customer: *"Advised mark may not lift."*

### 5.6 Measurements

Curtains, drapes, tablecloths and anything else where length matters are **measured at intake, and the measurement is written on the docket**, in millimetres, taken from the top of the heading tape to the bottom of the hem, with the customer watching you do it.

Relaxation shrinkage of up to 3% is normal and inherent in a hung cotton or linen curtain and is not a cleaning fault, but you can only say that if you know what the drop was on the way in. One pair measured at 2,650 mm at intake and 2,610 mm on return is a 1.5% change and a conversation you win. The same pair with no intake measurement is a conversation you lose.

Household textile work also requires Form MSDC-F04, the drapery advice, signed at intake. It sets out shrinkage, sun rot, lining separation and the fact that curtains often hang differently after cleaning until they settle.

## 6. The care label

### 6.1 Finding it and reading it

Find the label before you decide the method. It is normally in the left side seam about hip height, at the neck, in the waistband, or inside a pocket bag. On trousers, check the waistband and the left side seam. On curtains, check the top corner behind the heading tape, where there usually is not one.

Read it. Then read it out to the customer if it says anything unusual, because that is the moment to have the conversation rather than after the fact.

Care labelling in Australia is governed by **AS/NZS 1957 Textiles — Care labelling**. The standard requires the label to specify a care method that is suitable for the garment **as a whole**, including its trim, its lining, its interfacing and its components. That last point is the one that matters at our counter. A gown labelled with a plain "P" but carrying dense plastic bugle beading has a label that does not account for the trim, and that is non-compliance with AS/NZS 1957. It does not make the garment safe to clean, and it does not make us liable when the trim fails — but it does mean the label cannot be relied on, so the garment is at-risk under clause 7 no matter how reassuring the symbol looks.

When that is the case, write it on the docket in those words: *"Care label does not account for beaded trim — non-compliant with AS/NZS 1957."*

### 6.2 The symbols

There are five basic shapes. Learn the shapes first and the modifiers second.

| Symbol | What it governs | Detail and modifiers |
|---|---|---|
| **Washtub** | Domestic washing | A number inside gives the maximum wash temperature in °C. Dots may be used instead. One bar beneath = mild / permanent press. Two bars = very mild / delicate. A hand in the tub = hand wash only. Crossed out = do not wash. |
| **Triangle** | Bleaching | Plain triangle = any bleach may be used. Two diagonal lines inside = oxygen (non-chlorine) bleach only. Crossed out = do not bleach. |
| **Square** | Drying | A circle inside the square = tumble drying. One dot = low heat, two dots = normal heat, three dots = high. Crossed circle inside the square = do not tumble dry. A vertical line = line dry. A horizontal line = dry flat. A diagonal line in the top corner = dry in the shade. |
| **Circle** | Professional textile care | The letter inside gives the permitted medium. A bar beneath modifies the process. Crossed out = do not dry clean. |
| **Circle — P** | Perchloroethylene, and every solvent permitted under F | Union XL-800, normal process. A barred **P** means a reduced process — shorter cycle, reduced mechanical action, lower drying temperature. |
| **Circle — F** | Hydrocarbon and similar solvents **only**. Perchloroethylene is **not** permitted. | Realstar HM-450. A barred **F** means reduced process on the same machine. |
| **Circle — W** | Professional wet cleaning | Speed Queen washers on the wet clean programme, with the appropriate bar restriction. |
| **Iron** | Ironing and pressing | One dot = maximum 110 °C, no steam in most cases. Two dots = maximum 150 °C. Three dots = maximum 200 °C. Crossed out = do not iron. Crossed steam lines beneath the iron = do not steam. |

**The three rules that matter at the counter:**

1. **A bar means gentler.** One bar reduced, two bars very gentle. If in doubt, treat one bar as two.
2. **A cross means never.** A crossed circle is not a suggestion. If the garment must be cleaned and the circle is crossed, it goes to at-risk and an authorisation, or it is declined.
3. **F never means P.** A garment labelled F that goes into perc is a claim we cannot defend, cannot insure against, and have already paid once — $640 in 2025, a fused jacket whose fronts delaminated.

### 6.3 When the label is missing, cut out, illegible or wrong

| Situation | What you do |
|---|---|
| No label at all | The garment is at-risk under clause 7. Authorisation required. Record *"no care label present"*. |
| Label cut out | Same as no label. Ask the customer why it was cut out — usually it scratched — and write the answer down. |
| Illegible, faded or washed away | Treat as no label, unless you can read the circle and its modifiers with complete certainty. Half a symbol is no symbol. |
| Label contradicts the fabric | Believe the fabric, not the label. A "machine wash 40" label sewn into a fused wool jacket is wrong, and following it will destroy the garment. Route to the gentler of the two options and note the contradiction on the docket. |
| Two labels that disagree | Follow the more restrictive of the two. |
| Label in a language you cannot read | The symbols are international and are the same in every language. Read the symbols and ignore the words. |
| Retailer's label only, no care label | No care label. At-risk. |

Never guess a method and then write it on the route sheet as though it had come from a label. Write **"no care label — method by inspection"**, say which fibre you believe it to be and why, and let the plant see that a judgement was made rather than a fact recorded.

## 7. At-risk garments

A garment is at-risk if any one of the following is true. This is a list, not a judgement call. If it is on the list, it is at-risk, and clauses 8, 9 and 10 follow automatically.

| At-risk feature | What specifically can go wrong |
|---|---|
| **Beading and sequins** | Plastic beads and sequins cloud, go matt, soften, dissolve or lose their surface coating in solvent. Glass beads generally survive; plastic frequently does not, and no label tells you which you have. The thread holding the beading can also dissolve, dropping beads that were otherwise sound. Bugle beads are worse than round. |
| **Applied prints, transfers, foils, flock** | Lift at the edges, crack across the flex points, go tacky, or transfer onto the panel they are folded against. Heat in finishing finishes off anything the solvent started. Screen prints on knitwear are particularly prone. |
| **PU, PVC and coated fabrics** | The coating separates from its backing, goes sticky, crazes into a fine crackle or lifts in sheets. Both solvent and heat do it, and an older coating will do it without either. Very often labelled as though the coating were not there at all. |
| **Bonded and fused constructions** | Fusible interfacing in collars, cuffs, plackets, front panels and waistbands delaminates, leaving bubbling and rippling that no amount of pressing will remove. Common in cheaper tailoring, in anything over five years old, and in anything stored in a hot roof space. |
| **Leather and suede trim** | Colour transfer from the trim onto a pale shell, stiffening, shrinkage, loss of applied surface finish, and hardening at the edges. A leather trim can bleed into a cream garment in a single cycle. Whole leather garments go out to the specialist; they are never run in-house. |
| **Faux fur and pile fabrics** | Matting, flattening, permanent loss of lustre, and shrinkage of the knitted backing which distorts the whole panel. Very rarely recoverable once matted. |
| **Unlabelled garments** | Unknown fibre, unknown coating, unknown trim, unknown dye stability. Everything else in this table becomes possible and none of it is predictable. |
| **Garments over five years old** | Weakened fibres, perished elastic, shattered silk in linings, degraded interfacing, and oxidised invisible stains that appear as brown marks the first time heat is applied. Age is not a fault, but it removes the margin for error. |
| **Wedding gowns and formalwear** | Multiple substrates in one garment — mikado, tulle, horsehair, boning, glue-set appliqué — each behaving differently. Invisible sugar staining from the reception. Very high replacement values and an emotional weight that makes any conversation harder. |
| **Curtains, drapes and household textiles** | Sun-rotted face fabric that tears in handling, lining that has degraded at a different rate from the face, and relaxation shrinkage of up to 3% which is inherent to the cloth and is not a cleaning fault. Requires Form MSDC-F04 and a measurement under clause 5.6. |
| **Anything already damaged** | Cleaning does not cause the existing damage, but it will complete it. Split seams open further, worn areas go through, loose beading comes off, a cracked coating flakes. The customer will remember the garment as it went in. |
| **Anything the customer says is precious** | Sentimental, irreplaceable, a one-off, "it was my mother's". The value here is not in dollars and cannot be settled with money, which makes the conversation before cleaning more important, not less. |
| **Self-belts, sashes and detachable trims** | A dyed self-belt left attached crocks and bleeds onto the garment in the drum, and the belt buckle abrades the face fabric. **Every belt, sash and detachable trim comes off at intake, is docketed as its own piece, and is cleaned separately or not at all.** Where the care label itself says to remove the belt, quote the label on the docket. |
| **Collars showing product build-up** | Hair product, sunscreen and perspiration residue oxidise in perchloroethylene and leave a tide line across the collar and shoulders that is *lighter* than the surrounding cloth and cannot be put back. **Route to hydrocarbon, or pre-spot on the board first. Never send a built-up collar to perc untreated.** |
| **Pale and unstable dyes** | Deep red, navy and black on silk, and anything hand-dyed, may bleed. Test on an inside seam if there is any doubt, and note the test on the docket. |

## 8. The at-risk conversation

You are not warning the customer off their own garment. You are telling them what we know, before they decide, so the decision is theirs and it is informed. Done well, this conversation is the single strongest piece of customer service we offer, because almost nobody else does it.

### 8.1 How to raise it

Have the conversation **while the garment is on the bench**, pointing at the actual thing you are talking about. Pointing at a bead and saying what a bead does reads as expertise. The same words on the phone a week later read as an excuse.

Lead with the offer to show them, not with the risk:

> *"Before I book this in — can I show you something?"*

Then describe the mechanism, not the disaster. People accept a mechanism.

> *"These beads are plastic rather than glass. Plastic beads sometimes go cloudy in cleaning, because the solvent takes the surface off them. It isn't the fabric and it isn't the stitching — it's the bead itself, and there's no way to know in advance which ones will do it."*

Then say what we will do about it:

> *"We'd run it in the hydrocarbon machine, which is the gentlest thing we've got — gentler than the label actually asks for — in a net bag, cool, and on its own rather than in a load."*

Then be honest about the limit of that:

> *"That's the best anyone can do with it. I still can't promise the beads won't change."*

And then leave the decision with them:

> *"I'd rather tell you now than ring you in a week. It's your call."*

### 8.2 Words that work

- *"I'd rather tell you now than ring you in a week."*
- *"If it were mine I'd still clean it — but I'd want to know first."*
- *"The garment's fine. It's the trim I'm not certain about."*
- *"Nine times out of ten this is fine. I don't know which one this is."*
- *"We'll use the gentlest method we've got and I'll have the plant run it on its own."*
- *"This is what the form is for — it's not us washing our hands, it's a record that I told you."*

### 8.3 Words that must not be used

- **"It'll be fine."** It might not be, and you have just given a guarantee.
- **"We can't be held responsible."** Untrue as a matter of law, and it sounds like a shield going up.
- **"You'd be mad to clean this."** You have insulted the garment and the person who bought it.
- **"That's your risk, not ours."** Same problem, said faster.
- **"We do this all the time."** Then why are we having the conversation?

### 8.4 When the customer pushes back

Some customers will say another cleaner never mentioned any of this. Do not argue about the other cleaner and do not imply they were careless.

> *"That may well be, and it may well have been perfectly fine. I'm telling you what I can see today."*

Some will ask for a guarantee.

> *"I can guarantee the method and the care we take. What I can't guarantee is how a five-year-old coating behaves in solvent — nobody can. That's exactly what the form is for."*

Some will get annoyed and say we are just covering ourselves. The honest answer is yes, partly, and it is also the only way they get to make the choice.

> *"You're right that it protects us. It also means you're deciding, rather than finding out afterwards."*

Some will say just do it and they will take their chances — and then refuse to sign. That is a decline under clause 11. A verbal acceptance of risk is worth nothing and is not what this procedure allows.

### 8.5 The standing rule

**We would rather decline a garment than take one we cannot clean safely.**

Nobody at this business has ever been in trouble for turning work away. Several people have been in trouble for taking it. If you are standing at the counter genuinely unsure, the answer is not to take it and hope — it is to ring Sharon, or to decline it politely and keep the customer.

## 9. The at-risk authorisation

### 9.1 When it is mandatory

Form MSDC-F02, *Authorisation to Proceed — Garment Accepted at Customer's Risk*, is mandatory:

- for every garment falling under any line of clause 7, at both sites, without exception;
- whenever the customer's stated value of a single article exceeds $500;
- whenever a garment is going to an outside specialist;
- whenever the customer has told you the item is irreplaceable or sentimental;
- whenever the care label is absent, cut out or illegible; and
- whenever you have advised the customer that a mark may not lift and they want it attempted anyway.

If you are wondering whether it is mandatory, it is mandatory.

### 9.2 How it is completed

The form is generated from the docket in the app and printed at the counter, so that the customer, the docket number and the garment description are already correct and cannot be transcribed wrongly. Its blocks are set out in full at Appendix B.

Two parts are filled by hand and both matter.

**Condition at intake** is a numbered list of every pre-existing defect you found at clause 4. It should be specific and unflattering. This list is the whole point of the form. *"Finish worn through at both cuffs and along the collar fold. Right sleeve two shades lighter than the body. Stiffened area approximately 150 mm across the lower back where something has dried into the skin."* That is a useful list. *"Some wear"* is not.

**The risks** must be the risks of *this* garment, in plain words, numbered so they can be pointed at. *"Colour will change and may not return to the original shade. Further loss of finish at the cuffs and collar is likely. The mark on the lower back may not come out at all. The quilted panels may not take the re-finish evenly. Turnaround is three to four weeks, not the usual five days."*

**"Damage may occur" is not a risk statement.** It tells the customer nothing, it tells an assessor nothing, and it will not help anybody six weeks later.

Where a DLI TABS bulletin covers the failure mode, name it by title on the form and summarise its position in two or three sentences. For a leather garment that is *DLI TABS — Leather, Suede, Velvet & Napped Fabrics*; for beading and applied trim it is *DLI TABS — Prints, Embellishments, Trims & Notions*.

documents.background: How we take a garment in at both sites. Version 4, effective 1 March 2026. This is the procedure the "Tagging garments the Main Street way" training course was written from.
documents.text:
### 9.3 Signed before the garment is accepted, never after

The customer signs before the garment is accepted. Not at collection. Not when it comes back from the plant. Not when Peter has rung to say something has gone wrong.

**An authorisation signed after the event is worth nothing.** It is not a defence at law, it will not be accepted by the insurer, and producing one contaminates every honest record we hold. We have been here: in 2022 we paid $1,150 on a beaded jacket because the form was signed at collection instead of at intake, and the signature made the position worse rather than better.

The form does not exclude the consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law that cannot be excluded, and it says so in those words on its face. What it does is record that a specific risk was explained to a specific customer on a specific day, and that they chose to proceed. That is all it does. It is also, in practice, enough — see SOP 02 clause 6.

### 9.4 Where it is filed

The signed original is scanned into the app against the docket **before the garment leaves the counter**, so that the plant and the office can see it without going to look for paper. The paper original goes into the intake file at the site where it was signed, filed by docket number.

Kangaroo Flat originals travel to Bendigo with the garment on Dylan's run and are filed at Bendigo. A copy is offered to the customer every time, and most take it.

Authorisations are retained for seven years under SOP 02 clause 12, whether or not anything ever goes wrong.

## 10. Photographs

### 10.1 When they are mandatory

Photographs are mandatory for:

- every at-risk garment under clause 7;
- every garment taken on a signed MSDC-F02;
- every curtain and household textile job;
- every garment where the customer has raised a concern at the counter;
- every garment being sent out to a specialist; and
- every garment declined under clause 11, before it goes back over the counter.

They are taken on the site tablet, into the app, against the docket. Never on a personal phone, for the plain reason that a photograph on somebody's phone is not a business record and cannot be produced.

### 10.2 How many, and what must be in frame

**Minimum six.** For a leather jacket, a wedding gown or a set of curtains, expect eight to ten. There is no maximum and nobody has ever complained about too many.

1. The whole garment, front, flat on the bench, filling the frame.
2. The whole garment, back, flat on the bench.
3. The care label, close enough that every symbol can be read on screen.
4. Each area of pre-existing damage, close.
5. Each at-risk feature — the beading, the coating, the trim, the print, the worn cuff.
6. The docket number in frame with the garment in at least one shot, so the set cannot be attached to the wrong job.

**The scale reference.** The yellow 150 mm scale card lives on the counter at both sites and goes in frame beside anything photographed close. A mark photographed without a scale is a mark of unknown size, and "approximately this big" is not a measurement. Lay the card flat beside the mark, not on top of it.

Shoot in the daylight lamp or torch, not the ceiling light, and do not use flash on anything shiny — flash on beading photographs as a white blur and shows nothing.

### 10.3 Where they are stored

Photographs attach to the docket in the app and are visible to the plant, the office and the owner. They are retained for seven years under SOP 02 clause 12. They are never deleted, edited, filtered or cropped after the fact — a cropped photograph is worth less than no photograph, because it invites the question of what was cropped out.

## 11. Declining a garment

We decline in four situations, and only four.

1. **We cannot identify a safe method.** No label, an unidentifiable fibre or coating, and the customer will not sign an authorisation. If we do not know what it is and nobody will accept the risk, we cannot proceed.
2. **The garment will not survive the process.** Perished elastic, shattered silk, rotted lining, a coating already crazed and lifting, a seam holding by two threads, sun-rotted curtain fabric that tears in the hand. Cleaning will not have caused it, but cleaning will complete it, and the customer will remember only that they gave it to us intact.
3. **The soiling is something we are not equipped to handle safely.** Fuel or solvent contamination, sewage, heavy mould growth through the substrate, sharps in the seams, anything recovered from a fire scene. These are health and plant-safety questions, not textile ones.
4. **The expectation cannot be met.** The customer wants a guarantee we cannot give, or wants a set stain removed and has said they will accept nothing less than complete removal.

### How to say it

Short, warm, honest about the reason, and always with somewhere for them to go next.

> *"I'm not going to take this one, and I'll tell you why. The coating on the shoulders has already started to lift, and cleaning will lift the rest of it. I don't want to hand you back something worse than what you gave me. What I'd suggest is ..."*

Then suggest something real: a specialist we know, an alteration Anh can do, a re-line, airing and brushing rather than cleaning, or simply leaving it alone until it has to be cleaned. A customer who leaves with advice and no invoice comes back. A customer who leaves with a ruined garment does not.

Record the decline and the reason in the app against the customer, and photograph the garment before it goes back over the counter. If they take it to the other site next week, we need to know what was said this week.

## 12. Handover to the plant

### 12.1 Tagging

Every piece is tagged before it leaves the counter with its docket-and-piece number — B-24118/1 — on the standard tag. Pin at the neck, the waistband or an inside seam. Never through the face fabric of a delicate garment, never through beading, never through a coating, and never through a print.

Coloured tabs on the tag set the route at a glance:

| Tab | Route |
|---|---|
| No tab | Perchloroethylene, Union XL-800, standard process |
| Green | Hydrocarbon, Realstar HM-450 |
| Blue | Wet clean, Speed Queen |
| **Red** | **At-risk. Do not run without reading the authorisation.** |
| White | Send-out to an outside specialist |

A red tab always travels with a green tab or a blue tab as well, because at-risk is a condition, not a method.

### 12.2 The route sheet

The route sheet prints per docket and travels with the garments to the plant. A plant operator must be able to see, without asking anybody and without going back to the counter:

- the docket number and every piece number;
- the article, colour and brand;
- the care label exactly as read at intake, including bars and crosses;
- the method chosen and the machine;
- every pre-existing defect recorded at clause 5;
- every stain, its location, its size and its likely class;
- whether an authorisation exists and its number;
- whether photographs exist; and
- any special instruction — *belt removed and cleaned separately*, *do not press*, *run alone*, *hand finish*, *no steam on trim*, *collar pre-spot before load*.

**If the route sheet does not say it, the plant does not know it.** Peter is not a mind reader and Marco is finishing forty pieces an hour. Anything you decided at the counter that changes what the plant does must be written where the plant will read it.

### 12.3 If the plant disagrees with the intake decision

Peter, Marco or Julie may look at a garment and disagree with the method, the risk assessment or the promise made at the counter. That is the point of having them look, and it is not a criticism of the counter.

1. The operator **stops** and does not run the garment.
2. The garment goes on the **query rail** with the route sheet annotated — what they think and why, in one line, with their initials and the date.
3. The operator tells Sharon the same day. Sharon rules on the method.
4. If the method changes in a way the customer would care about — a longer turnaround, a different machine, a risk that was not discussed — **the customer is rung before anything is run**, and a fresh MSDC-F02 is raised if the new risk is not covered by the one on file.
5. If Sharon and the operator do not agree, Karen decides. Nobody runs the garment in the meantime.
6. The outcome is written back onto the route sheet and into the docket, so the record shows the query and its resolution.

A garment sitting on the query rail overnight becomes a phone call to the customer about the collection date. It does not become a silence.

## 13. Drop store specifics — Kangaroo Flat

Kangaroo Flat is a 24 m² drop store in Lansell Square: a counter, racking, a tablet and a hand basin. No plant, no machine, no solvent, no second opinion and nobody else on the floor. Rebecca works alone, and on a Saturday morning the centre is busy.

Everything in this procedure applies at Kangaroo Flat exactly as it applies at Bendigo. In addition:

**Do not accept an at-risk garment on your own judgement.** The rule is three steps, in this order, and there is no version of it where the garment is booked in first and the call is made later.

1. **Photograph it.** The full clause 10 set, on the tablet, into the app against the docket, with the yellow scale card in frame on every close shot. Do this while the customer is standing there, because you may need to turn the garment over and ask questions.
2. **Ring Bendigo.** (03) 5443 8817. Ask for Sharon; ask for Karen if Sharon is not on the floor. Describe what you can see in the order of clause 4.2. The photographs are already in the app, so whoever answers can be looking at the same garment while you talk.
3. **Do what you are told.** If the answer is take it on an authorisation, raise MSDC-F02 and set out the risks you have been given, in the words you have been given. If the answer is decline, decline it under clause 11 and say so kindly. If nobody answers the phone, the garment is **not accepted** — take the customer's number, tell them Sharon will ring them today, and make sure the message is left.

This is not a lack of confidence in the counter. It is that one person, alone, with a queue behind a customer and a leather jacket on the bench, should not have to carry a decision of that size — and does not have to.

Docket K-09104, taken on 24 August 2026, is the model and is worth reading in the app. A five-year-old lambskin biker jacket with the finish worn through at the cuffs, a sun-faded right sleeve and a set mark on the lower back. Rebecca stopped the booking, took nine photographs including the scale on the back mark, and rang Bendigo rather than take the decision at the counter. Karen looked at the photographs, and the garment was accepted on a signed authorisation naming colour change, further finish loss and the possibility that the mark would not come out, and sent to the specialist rather than run in-house. Stop, photograph, ring, then act.

## 14. Common failures

Six intake mistakes that have actually cost this business money. Every one of them is in this procedure somewhere, and every one of them was a step somebody skipped because it was busy.

| # | What happened | What it cost | The correct action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A dyed self-belt was left attached to a dress. In the drum the belt crocked onto the skirt and left colour transfer across the front. | $310 settlement | Belt removed at intake, docketed as its own piece, cleaned separately or not at all (clause 7). |
| 2 | Collar build-up was not noticed and not noted. The jacket went to perc untreated, the residue oxidised, and the collar and shoulders came back lighter than the body. | $420 settlement | Build-up found at clause 4.2 step 1, recorded, and the garment routed to hydrocarbon or pre-spotted on the board (clause 7). |
| 3 | Pockets were not emptied. A lip balm went through a perc load and marked eleven garments belonging to nine customers. | $780 and eleven apologies | Every pocket emptied by hand and *"pockets emptied"* written on the docket, nil included (clause 5.4). |
| 4 | The care label was not read. A fused jacket labelled **F** was run in perc and the front panels delaminated. | $640 settlement | The circle and its letter read and recorded, and F never routed to perc (clause 6.2). |
| 5 | Four pairs of curtains were accepted with no drop measurement and no Form MSDC-F04. The customer complained of shrinkage and we had nothing to compare against. | Three weeks of argument and a free re-hem | Drop measured in millimetres at intake with the customer watching, written on the docket, and the drapery advice signed (clause 5.6). |
| 6 | An at-risk authorisation on a beaded jacket was signed at collection rather than at intake, after the beading had already dulled. | $1,150 settlement | Signed before the garment was accepted, or the garment declined (clause 9.3). |

Five of the six were a line that was not written on a docket. None of the six was a machine fault. That is the whole argument of clause 2, in a table.

---

## Appendix A — Intake checklist card (Form MSDC-F01)

Laminated, on the counter at both sites, beside the terminal.

1. Garments out of the bag and flat on the bench.
2. Daylight lamp or torch on.
3. Count the pieces out loud, twice, with the customer.
4. Find the care label. Read the circle, the bars and the crosses.
5. Work the order: collar, shoulders, cuffs, front, back, hem, lining, pockets, closures, trims.
6. Empty every pocket by hand. Write "pockets emptied" even when nil.
7. Remove every belt, sash and detachable trim. Docket it separately.
8. Write every defect: where, what, how big.
9. Write every stain: where, size, colour, likely class. Promise nothing.
10. Measure anything where length matters.
11. At-risk under clause 7? Talk it through, photograph, authorise, red tab.
12. Confirm the collection date and the phone number.
13. Tag each piece, print the route sheet, rack it.

If you are unsure at any point: stop, and ring Sharon on (03) 5443 8817.

## Appendix B — Authorisation to proceed (Form MSDC-F02)

The form prints with the following blocks, in this order.

**Heading line:** AUTHORISATION TO PROCEED — GARMENT ACCEPTED AT CUSTOMER'S RISK

1. **Identification.** Customer name. Docket number. Site. Date. Staff member.
2. **The garment.** Full description — type, brand, colour, style, construction — and the customer's stated value.
3. **The care label.** Quoted exactly as it reads. Whether it is present, absent, illegible or cut out. Any non-compliance with AS/NZS 1957 noted, with the reason.
4. **Condition at intake.** A numbered list of every pre-existing defect found at clause 4. Specific and unflattering. This list is the whole point of the form.
5. **What we propose to do.** The method, the machine or the specialist, and whether treatment is whole-garment or localised.
6. **The risks.** A numbered list, specific to this garment, in plain words, including the turnaround where it differs from the standard five days.
7. **The industry position.** Where a DLI TABS bulletin covers the failure mode, it is named by title and its position summarised in two or three sentences.
8. **Authorisation wording.** That the customer has read the above; that they accept the garment is accepted at their risk; that they authorise us to proceed; and that this does not exclude the guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law that cannot be excluded.
9. **Signatures.** Customer signature, printed name and date. Staff signature, printed name and date.

## Appendix C — Care symbol reference (Form MSDC-F03)

**Washtub — domestic washing.** The number inside is the maximum temperature in °C. One bar beneath means a mild process, two bars a very mild process. A hand in the tub means hand wash only. Crossed out means do not wash.

**Triangle — bleaching.** Plain means any bleach may be used. Two diagonal lines inside mean oxygen (non-chlorine) bleach only. Crossed out means do not bleach.

**Square — drying.** A circle inside means tumble drying: one dot low heat, two dots normal, three dots high. A crossed circle inside means do not tumble dry. A vertical line means line dry, a horizontal line means dry flat, and a diagonal line in the top corner means dry in the shade.

**Circle — professional textile care.** **P** means perchloroethylene and every solvent permitted under F — the Union XL-800. **F** means hydrocarbon only and perc is not permitted — the Realstar HM-450. **W** means professional wet cleaning. One bar beneath means a mild process, two bars a very mild process, and a crossed circle means do not dry clean.

**Iron — ironing and pressing.** One dot is a maximum of 110 °C, two dots 150 °C, three dots 200 °C. Crossed out means do not iron. Crossed steam lines beneath the iron mean do not steam.

**Remember three things:** a bar means gentler, a cross means never, and F never means P.

---

*Issued by Karen Whitfield, Owner, Main Street Dry Cleaners, Aveline Holdings Pty Ltd ACN 617 903 558, Shop 4, 118 Hargreaves Street, Bendigo VIC 3550. Version 4, effective 1 March 2026. Review due March 2027.*

documents.text:
# SOP 02 — Handling a Complaint, Assessing a Claim and Escalating It

**Document number:** MSDC-SOP-02
**Version:** 3
**Effective:** 1 March 2026
**Owner:** Karen Whitfield, Owner
**Approved by:** Karen Whitfield, Owner
**Review due:** March 2027
**Applies at:** Shop 4, 118 Hargreaves Street, Bendigo · Shop 12, Lansell Square, 233 High Street, Kangaroo Flat
**Related documents:** MSDC-SOP-01 Counter Intake, Inspection and At-Risk Tagging · Form MSDC-F02 Authorisation to Proceed · Form MSDC-F10 Problem Report · Form MSDC-F11 Assessment Record · Meridian Underwriting business pack policy MDC-BP-4471822

### Revision history

| Ver | Date | Author | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 01/09/2016 | K. Whitfield | First issue. Complaint handling separated from intake. |
| 2 | 01/02/2022 | K. Whitfield | International Fair Claims Guide adopted as the settlement basis. Depreciation worked examples added. Authority limits set. |
| 3 | 01/03/2026 | K. Whitfield | Four named outcomes introduced. Phrases that must never be used added at clause 2. "Do not touch it yet" added at clause 4. Insurance clause rewritten around the bailee's sub-limit. Monthly claim review added at clause 13. |

---

## 1. Purpose, scope and who may do what

This procedure covers what happens from the moment a customer tells us something is wrong with a garment to the moment the matter is closed and filed. It applies at both sites and to every complaint about a garment, whether or not the customer uses the word "claim", and whether the garment is worth $40 or $3,200.

It does not cover complaints about price, turnaround or service, which Sharon handles at her discretion and does not need this procedure for. It starts the moment a garment is put on the counter and something is said to be wrong with it.

### 1.1 Who does what

| Role | Authority |
|---|---|
| **Counter staff** — Emma, Chloe, Rebecca, and Sharon when she is on the front | Take the report. Calm the customer. Record the facts. Take the garment in and hold it. **No admission of liability, no denial of liability, no offer of money, no estimate of blame.** |
| **Sharon Delaney, Shop Manager** | Assesses. Pulls the docket, the intake record, the photographs, the machine log and the route sheet. Examines the garment. Forms a recommendation under clause 6. May settle up to **$250** and may authorise a re-clean, a re-press or an alteration at our cost without reference to Karen. |
| **Peter Nguyen, plant operator** | Provides the plant facts — what machine, what programme, what load, what the log says. Does not decide fault and does not speak to the customer about it. |
| **Anh Tran, alterations** | Advises whether a repair, re-hem, re-line or re-bead is possible and what it would cost us. |
| **Karen Whitfield, Owner** | Decides **anything over $250**, **anything that goes out in writing**, anything involving the insurer, anything involving Consumer Affairs Victoria, and anything where Sharon and the customer are stuck. |

**Anything in writing is Karen's.** A letter, an email that sets out a position, a text message that concedes or refuses anything — all of it goes out over Karen's name, in the house voice, and none of it is sent by anyone else. A friendly email saying "we'll have a look and get back to you" is fine and is not a position.

### 1.2 The two standing principles

1. **Nobody admits or denies liability at the counter.** Not the counter staff, not Sharon, not Peter if he happens to walk through. The counter takes the report. The assessment decides the position. Those are two different jobs done by two different people at two different times, and collapsing them is how a $120 problem becomes a $900 one.
2. **The customer is told the truth, once we know it.** When we are at fault we say so plainly and in the first paragraph. We do not hedge, we do not write "we regret that you feel", and we do not make people fight for what they are owed. That is a commercial decision as much as a moral one: the customers we settle honestly come back, and the ones we grind down go to Consumer Affairs Victoria.

## 2. The first ninety seconds

Somebody puts a garment on the counter and they are unhappy. Perhaps very unhappy. What happens in the next minute and a half decides whether this is a twenty-minute matter or a six-week one.

### 2.1 What to do

**Stop what you are doing.** Put down the hangers. If there is a queue, acknowledge it — *"I'll be with you shortly"* to the queue — and then give this customer your attention.

**Take the garment.** Physically take it, lay it on the bench and look at it while they talk. Looking at the garment while they speak signals that you are taking it seriously, and it starts the assessment.

**Let them finish.** Do not interrupt, do not correct a fact, and do not start explaining. People who are angry about a garment are usually angry about something else as well, and they need to get to the end of it. It takes less time than you think.

**Say the three things.** In this order:

> *"I'm sorry — that's not what you should have got back from us."*
>
> *"Let me write down exactly what's happened, and then I'll have Sharon look at it properly."*
>
> *"Can I keep the garment here so she can see it? I'll give you a receipt for it."*

The first sentence is an apology for the *situation*, not an admission of fault, and it is the single most useful thing anybody says in this procedure. "That's not what you should have got back from us" is true whether the fault is ours, the manufacturer's or nobody's.

**Move them off the front counter if you can.** At Bendigo, the end of the counter by the alterations window. It takes the audience away and drops the temperature immediately.

**Get the garment onto the hold rail.** Bagged, tagged with the docket number and the date, not touched again until clause 4 and 5 have happened.

### 2.2 What must never be said

These six phrases are prohibited. Not discouraged — prohibited. Each of them has cost this business money.

1. **"You signed for it."** The at-risk authorisation is not a waiver, it does not exclude the consumer guarantees, and saying this makes us look as though we think it does. It also tells the customer that we knew there was a risk and are now hiding behind a signature, which is the opposite of why the form exists.
2. **"That's not our fault."** Said before anyone has assessed anything, it is a guess, and if the assessment goes the other way we have to climb back down from it. Even when it turns out to be true, it is the wrong sentence — the right one is a technical explanation, later, in writing.
3. **"That's just wear and tear."** It might be. But it is a finding, not a greeting, and it sounds like a brush-off delivered across a counter.
4. **"The label said dry clean, so there's nothing we could have done."** Following a care label is not automatically a defence, and this sentence gives away the whole assessment before it has been made.
5. **"You'll have to take that up with the manufacturer."** Even where the fault is a manufacturing one, this is our customer standing in front of us. We are the ones who write the letter they take back to the retailer. We do not send people away.
6. **"Everyone gets that with this fabric."** If everybody gets it, we should have said so at intake, and we did not.

Two more that are not prohibited but should be avoided: *"I'll have to ask my manager"* (say *"Sharon will look at it herself"* instead, which sounds like an assessment rather than a delay), and *"we've never had this happen before"* (unverifiable, and irrelevant to them).

### 2.3 Taking the heat out

- **Lower your voice.** People match volume. It works every time and it costs nothing.
- **Use their name** once you have it from the docket.
- **Agree with what is true.** *"You're right, that mark wasn't there on the docket."* Agreeing with a true thing early buys enormous credit for disagreeing with something later.
- **Give a next step with a time on it.** *"Sharon's in tomorrow from seven. She'll look at it in the morning and I'll have her ring you before midday."* Vagueness is what makes people escalate.
- **Do not defend the plant.** You do not know yet, and it is not your job.
- **If they will not calm down**, do not argue and do not match them. *"I can see how frustrating this is. Let me get the details down and get it to Sharon today."* If they are abusive, Sharon or Karen takes over; nobody on this counter has to absorb that.

### 2.4 The rule

**Nobody admits or denies liability at the counter.** Say what we will do next and when. Do not say who is at fault, because you do not know, and the person who has to unsay it is Karen.

## 3. Taking the report

Form MSDC-F10, the problem report, is raised in the app while the customer is still there. Not afterwards.

### 3.1 The fields, and why each one matters

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Docket number | Everything else hangs off it — the intake record, the route sheet, the machine log, the photographs. Without it there is no assessment. |
| Customer name and contact | We will need to ring them, probably more than once. |
| Site | Which counter took the garment in, and which counter is taking the complaint. They are often different. |
| Date reported, and by whom | Fixes the timeline and starts the clock on our own response times. |
| Date cleaned | The gap between cleaning and complaint is itself evidence. A complaint on collection day and a complaint six weeks later are different animals. |
| Garment description | Type, colour, brand, style, and anything that identifies this garment from any other. |
| Care label as it reads now | Read it again yourself. Do not copy the intake record — check whether it agrees. |
| What happened, in the customer's words | Clause 3.2. |
| What you can see | Your own observation, kept separate from theirs. |
| Where the damage is, and how big | Location, size in millimetres, and whether it is on one part or all over. |
| Prior cleaning history | By us, and elsewhere. Ask. Damage from a previous clean by somebody else surfaces on the second clean surprisingly often. |
| Value, and where that figure comes from | "It cost $1,250 at David Jones" is a fact. "It's worth about a thousand" is an opinion. Record which one you were given. |
| Purchase date and place | Needed for Table I and Table II under clause 8. Ask for the receipt if they have it; most people do not, and that is fine. |
| What the customer wants | Clause 3.3. |
| Whether an authorisation exists | Look it up while they are there. |
| Photographs taken today | Clause 4. |
| Where the garment is now | Hold rail, bagged, tagged. |

### 3.2 Writing "what happened" so it is useful

Two accounts go into the report and they are kept apart.

**The customer's account, in their words.** As close to verbatim as you can manage. Not tidied up, not summarised into "customer alleges damage".

> *"She says the jacket went in with the trousers on 22 May, she collected on 27 May, and she noticed on the Saturday when she went to wear it that the collar and both shoulders are lighter than the rest. She says it's obvious in daylight and she can't wear it to work."*

Their words matter because their story rarely changes and any change in it later is significant, and because a customer who reads back their own words feels heard.

**Your account, in yours.** What you can see on the bench, in the daylight lamp, described the way clause 5 of SOP 01 describes anything:

> *"Collar and the tops of both shoulders are visibly lighter than the body of the jacket and than the trousers. There is a defined line across the shoulder seam. Colour change is even on both sides. No fibre damage visible, no thinning, no marking."*

Keep the two apart in the record. When Sharon assesses, she needs to know which parts she is being told and which parts have been observed.

### 3.3 What the customer actually wants

Ask, and write down the answer in their words:

> *"What would you like us to do about it?"*

It is a genuine question and the answer is frequently much smaller than anybody assumed. Two out of three people want the garment put right, or a clean redone, or an apology and an explanation they can understand. The minority who want money often want less than the full replacement price. You cannot settle a complaint you have not asked the shape of.

Record it exactly. *"Wants it replaced — says it cost $890 at Myer in October 2023."* *"Wants the mark out, doesn't want money."* *"Wants to know how it happened."* *"Wants a refund of the cleaning charge and nothing else."* Do not translate a request for an explanation into a claim for compensation. That is how small things become big ones.

Do not promise the outcome. What you say is:

> *"I've written that down and Sharon will have it in the morning. I can't tell you today what we'll be able to do, but somebody will ring you by tomorrow afternoon either way."*

## 4. Do not touch it yet

**The garment is not re-cleaned, spotted, pressed, brushed, steamed or worked on in any way until it has been assessed under clause 5 and photographed.** Not by the counter, not by the plant, not by anybody being helpful.

This is the rule most often broken with the best intentions, and it is the most expensive one to break.

**Why:**

- **Re-cleaning destroys the evidence.** Once a garment has been through a second cycle nobody can say what the first one did. Every subsequent conversation — with the customer, with Karen, with the insurer, with a manufacturer, with Consumer Affairs Victoria — becomes an argument about a garment that no longer exists in the condition complained of.
- **It usually makes it worse.** A delaminated fusible does not re-bond. A cloudy bead does not re-clarify. Colour that has migrated migrates further. A shrunken wool jumper shrinks again. Of the failure modes we see, the number that improve with a second clean is close to zero.
- **It removes the comparison.** Clause 5.4 depends on comparing an affected area with an unaffected area of the same garment. A second full clean often changes both.
- **It looks like concealment.** A garment that has been quietly re-processed before anybody photographed it is a bad fact, and it is a bad fact even when nothing was being concealed.
- **It pre-empts the decision.** Re-cleaning is a remedy. Offering a remedy before assessing is an admission, and it is Sharon's decision or Karen's, not the counter's.

**What to do instead.** Bag it, tag it with the docket number and today's date, and put it on the hold rail. Photograph it today, under clause 4.1. Then leave it alone.

### 4.1 Photographs at the point of complaint

Taken the same day, on the site tablet, into the app against the docket, alongside the intake photographs if there are any.

1. The whole garment, front and back, flat, in daylight.
2. The damage, close, with the yellow 150 mm scale card in frame.
3. The same detail on an unaffected part of the same garment, for comparison — the underside of a collar, an inside seam, a facing, the trousers of the same suit.
4. The care label, again, as it reads today.
5. Any maker's or retailer's label, and any size or fibre-content label.

The comparison shot at point 3 is the one people forget and the one that decides the most claims. A photograph of a lightened collar means little on its own; the same photograph beside the unchanged trousers of the same suit means a great deal.

### 4.2 The one permitted exception

If the garment is wet, contaminated or actively deteriorating — a dye that is still bleeding, mould that is growing — Sharon may direct a stabilising step. She rings Karen first, the reason is written on the assessment record, and photographs are taken before and after. That is the only exception, and it is a direction from Sharon, never an initiative from the counter or the plant.

## 5. The assessment

Sharon assesses. The assessment is a paper exercise and a physical one, and it is recorded on Form MSDC-F11.

### 5.1 What to pull, and what each thing tells you

| Record | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **The docket** | Who took it, at which site, on what date, what service was asked for, what was promised, what was charged. It also tells you who to ask, because the person who inspected it is named on it. |
| **The intake record** (SOP 01 clause 5) | The condition of the garment before we touched it. Pre-existing damage, worn areas, previous repairs, existing stains and their class, whether the pockets were emptied, whether the belt came off. This is the most valuable single record we hold, and its absence is itself a finding. |
| **The intake photographs** | The same thing, but unarguable. Compare like with like — the same panel, the same seam, the same trim. |
| **The care label as recorded at intake** | What we were permitted to do. Circle, letter, bars, crosses. Then check it against the label on the garment now, because a mis-read label at intake is a real cause of real damage. |
| **The route sheet** | What the counter told the plant to do, and any special instruction — belt removed, run alone, do not press, collar pre-spot. If the instruction is not on the sheet, it did not reach the plant. |
| **The machine log** | What the plant actually did. Machine, programme number, load composition, cycle length, bath time, extract speed, drying temperature, cool-down, operator, and the time and date. The Union XL-800 and the Realstar HM-450 both log by cycle; the Speed Queens log programme and temperature. This is where a garment run at 40 °C on a programme that should have been 30 °C shows up, in black and white, with nobody's memory involved. |
| **Any MSDC-F02 authorisation** | Whether the risk that eventuated is the risk that was named, and — critically — whether it was signed before the garment was accepted. |
| **The customer's file** | Prior work, prior complaints, prior settlements. Relevant to context, never to the merits. |

Read the machine log before you form a view. It is the only record in the building that nobody had an opinion while making.

documents.title: SOP 02 — complaint handling — Examining the garment, What a "major failure" means here, Defend
documents.background: What happens when someone puts a garment on the counter unhappy. Version 3, effective 1 March 2026. Counter staff take the report, Sharon assesses, Karen decides anything over $250 or anything going in writing.
documents.text:
### 5.2 Examining the garment

In daylight — the north window at the Bendigo counter in the morning, or the 6,500 K daylight lamp. Never under the plant fluoros, which flatten colour and hide exactly the differences you are looking for.

Flat on the bench, right way out first, then inside out. Handle it as little as possible and do not brush, pick or rub at anything.

Work the same order as SOP 01 clause 4.2 — collar, shoulders, cuffs, front, back, hem, lining, pockets, closures, trims — because you are looking for what *else* is going on as much as for the thing complained of.

### 5.3 What you are looking at

Distinguish between these, because they have different causes and different outcomes:

- **Colour change** — lighter, darker, duller, yellowed, or shifted in hue. Even or uneven. Bounded by a line, or graduated.
- **Dimensional change** — shrinkage, stretching, twisting, distortion of a panel or a hem.
- **Surface change** — pilling, matting, loss of nap, shine, glazing, loss of a finish or coating.
- **Structural failure** — a split seam, a hole, a tear, a broken thread, delamination.
- **Deposit or transfer** — colour that has arrived from somewhere else, a redeposited soil, a lint or fibre transfer.
- **Component failure** — a bead, a sequin, a button, a zip, a buckle, an interfacing. The garment is fine and the part is not.

Name it in those terms on the assessment record. "Ruined" is not a finding; *"uneven colour loss across the collar and both shoulder tops, bounded by a defined line at the shoulder seam, no fibre damage"* is.

### 5.4 Comparing against an unaffected part

This is the technique that decides more assessments than any other, and it takes two minutes.

Find a part of the *same garment* that has not been affected and compare it, side by side, in the same light. The underside of a collar against its top. An inside facing against an outer panel. A pocket flap against the body. The trousers of the same suit against the jacket. A seam allowance against the face fabric.

What the comparison tells you:

- **Uniform change across the whole garment** points to the process — solvent, temperature, mechanical action.
- **Change only where the garment is exposed to wear, light or contact** points to wear, sun or use, not to us. Collar, cuffs, shoulders, elbows and seat are the wear points.
- **Change bounded by a hard line** points to something that was applied or deposited on the garment — a spill, a residue, a previous treatment — and not to the bath.
- **Change on one component only** points to that component.

Photograph the comparison. It is the shot that persuades a customer, and it is the shot that persuades an insurer.

## 6. Where does fault sit

Six questions, in this order. Answer them on the assessment record before you go anywhere near a number.

**Question 1 — Was the care label followed?**
Read the circle, the letter and the bars as recorded at intake, and check what the machine log says we did. If the label permitted F and we ran P, stop: that is our failure and the answer is settle. If the label permitted P and we ran P at the standard process where a bar required a reduced one, stop: same answer.

**Question 2 — Was the method actually gentler than the label allowed?**
This is the strongest defensive fact we have and it is worth being precise about. A garment labelled **P** that we ran in hydrocarbon on the beaded programme — four minute bath, extract capped at 200 rpm, dried at 38 °C with an extended cool-down, run alone rather than in a load — was cleaned materially more gently than its own label permitted. If the garment failed anyway, it did not fail because of what we chose.

**Question 3 — Was there an at-risk authorisation, and does it cover this?**
Three separate sub-questions. Does an MSDC-F02 exist? Was it signed *before* the garment was accepted? And does it name *this* failure mode — not damage in general, but this? An authorisation that names clouding of the beading and a garment whose beading has clouded is a strong position. An authorisation that says "damage may occur" is not. An authorisation signed at collection is worth nothing at all and is not to be relied on in any letter (SOP 01 clause 9.3).

**Question 4 — Is the failure mode a known fabric or manufacturing fault?**
Some things fail in cleaning because of how they were made, and the industry literature says so. Plastic bead coatings, fusible interfacings, applied prints, PU coatings, dye that was never fixed properly, a trim the care label never accounted for. Where the DLI TABS bulletins cover the mechanism, name the relevant bulletin by title on the assessment record and quote what it attributes the failure to. Where the care label did not account for a trim or a component, that is non-compliance with AS/NZS 1957 and it is the manufacturer's problem, not ours.

**Question 5 — Is it wear?**
Age, use, abrasion, sun, perspiration and previous cleaning all show up in the first clean after they have accumulated. Wear presents at the wear points, gradually, and shows on both sides symmetrically where both sides get the same use. Cleaning reveals wear; it does not cause it. But be careful with this answer, because it is the easiest one to reach for and the easiest to be wrong about. Do not give it unless the pattern of the damage supports it and the comparison at clause 5.4 backs it up.

**Question 6 — Is it something we did?**
The honest question, asked last so that it is asked properly. Was the collar built up and sent to perc untreated? Was the belt left on? Did the programme run at the wrong temperature? Was it pressed when the route sheet said not to? Was it packed in ordinary tissue instead of acid-free? The machine log and the route sheet answer most of these and they answer them without regard to anybody's feelings.

If the answer is yes, the answer is yes. We say so, we say so first, and we do not make the customer prove it.

### 6.1 The four outcomes

The six questions lead to one of four outcomes.

| Outcome | When it applies |
|---|---|
| **Defend** | Not our fault, and the fault sits with the garment, its manufacture, its trim or its labelling. We say so technically and we help the customer take it back to whoever sold it. |
| **Deny** | Not our fault, and there is nobody else to send them to — the damage is wear, age or an inherent characteristic of the cloth. We decline liability, explain why, and where we can, offer something practical that costs us little and helps them. |
| **Settle** | Our fault. We accept it, we calculate the adjusted value under clause 8, and we pay. |
| **Goodwill** | Nothing is damaged and nobody is at fault, but the customer has not had what they expected. We put it right at our cost and we do not treat it as a claim. |

### 6.2 The worked flow

1. Is the garment actually damaged, as opposed to not-as-expected? If not damaged, go to **goodwill**.
2. Did we depart from the care label, the route sheet or our own procedure? If yes, go to **settle**.
3. Does the machine log show a process error? If yes, go to **settle**.
4. Is the failure mode a known manufacturing, trim or labelling fault? If yes, and there is a retailer or maker to go back to, go to **defend**.
5. Is it wear, age or an inherent characteristic? If yes, go to **deny**, and look for something practical to offer.
6. Is there a signed authorisation, given before acceptance, naming this failure mode, and was the method at least as gentle as the label allowed? If yes, go to **defend**.
7. If you are genuinely between two outcomes, take it to Karen. The tie does not go to the business.

## 7. The Australian Consumer Law position

Everybody at this counter should be able to say this much accurately, because customers frequently say a version of it that is not quite right, and because it is the framework the whole procedure sits inside.

### 7.1 Section 60 — due care and skill

Under section 60 of the Australian Consumer Law, a supplier of services to a consumer guarantees that the services will be rendered **with due care and skill**.

What that means for us is that we promise a **competent job**, not a **perfect outcome**. It is a guarantee about the standard of our work — the method chosen, the process run, the attention given — and not a warranty that every garment will emerge exactly as it went in. If we identify the fibre correctly, read the label correctly, choose an appropriate method, run it correctly, and the garment fails anyway because of how it was made, we have met the guarantee.

Conversely, if we run a garment labelled F in perchloroethylene, we have not exercised due care and skill, and no amount of anything else will fix that.

### 7.2 A sign or a docket cannot exclude it

The consumer guarantees cannot be excluded, restricted or modified by contract. A sign on the wall, a line of small print on the docket, or a signature on Form MSDC-F02 does not remove the guarantee of due care and skill, and any attempt to say it does is itself a breach.

This is why nobody says *"you signed for it"* (clause 2.2). The authorisation is evidence that a risk was identified and explained and that the customer chose to proceed. It is good evidence and it decides real cases. What it is not, and never claims to be on its face, is a waiver.

### 7.3 Section 61 — fitness for a stated purpose

Section 61 adds a guarantee that where a consumer makes known the particular purpose for which the services are being acquired, or the result they want to achieve, the services and any product resulting from them will be reasonably fit for that purpose or of such a nature that they can reasonably be expected to achieve that result.

At our counter this bites whenever a customer tells us *why* they are having something cleaned and we take the work on that footing. *"I need this for a wedding on Saturday."* *"I want the mark on the back out — that's the whole reason I'm here."* *"This is going into a box for my daughter."*

Two consequences follow, both practical. First, **do not accept a stated purpose you cannot meet**: if the mark will not come out, say so at intake and write on the docket that you said so (SOP 01 clause 5.5). Second, **record the stated purpose** when there is one, because it changes what we have promised.

### 7.4 What a "major failure" means here

A failure is major, broadly, where a reasonable consumer would not have acquired the service had they known the extent of the problem, where the service is substantially unfit for its normal purpose or for the purpose made known and cannot easily be made fit within a reasonable time, or where the service creates an unsafe situation.

Where a failure is major, the consumer chooses the remedy — cancelling the service and getting a refund, or compensation for the drop in value. Where the failure is **not** major, the supplier chooses, and we may remedy it in a reasonable time by putting it right.

In our trade the practical line usually falls like this. A garment we have damaged so that it cannot reasonably be worn as it was — colour lost, shrunk out of size, delaminated — is a major failure, the customer chooses, and clause 8 tells us what the compensation figure is. A garment where a mark did not come out, or which needs re-cleaning or re-pressing, is normally not a major failure, and our remedy is to do it again properly, promptly and at our cost.

Never argue about whether something is major at the counter. Assess it, decide, and put the position in writing over Karen's name.

## 8. The International Fair Claims Guide

### 8.1 What it is and why we use it

The International Fair Claims Guide for Consumer Textile Products is the schedule the dry cleaning industry uses worldwide to put a value on a damaged garment. It is not law and it does not bind a customer. We use it for three reasons: it is consistent, so the same garment gets the same answer whoever assesses it; it is external, so the number is not something we invented to suit ourselves; and it is explainable, so a customer can see the working.

It has two parts. **Table I** gives an expected **life expectancy** for each class of article. **Table II** gives a **percentage of replacement cost** to be paid, according to how much of that life has been used and what condition the garment was in.

The principle is depreciated value, not replacement cost. A customer is entitled to be put back where they were — which is the value of a part-worn garment, not the price of a brand new one. Nobody enjoys hearing this, so the arithmetic must be shown, plainly, every time.

### 8.2 Table I — life expectancy

Life expectancy is the period over which an article of that class is expected to remain serviceable with normal use and care. Some representative entries:

| Article | Life expectancy |
|---|---|
| Suit — wool or wool blend | 3 years |
| Dress — fancy | 2 years |
| Dress — plain, everyday | 3 years |
| Jumper or cardigan — wool | 4 years |
| Overcoat — wool | 5 years |
| Wedding gown — after the wedding | 3 years |
| Leather or suede jacket | 4 years |
| Curtains and drapes, lined | 5 years |

Life expectancy is not a use-by date. A garment older than its life expectancy has not become worthless; it has become fully depreciated for the purposes of the Guide, and the settlement reflects that.

### 8.3 Table II — depreciation

Table II reads across two axes: how far into the life expectancy the garment is, expressed as an age band, and the condition it was in before we touched it — excellent, average or poor. The intersection gives the percentage of replacement cost payable.

The condition column is where the intake record earns its keep. "Excellent" and "average" are not opinions offered at the point of complaint; they are findings that ought to be supported by what was written on the docket at intake under SOP 01 clause 5.

### 8.4 A worked example

A wool jumper. Replacement cost $640, established from the customer's receipt.

1. **Table I.** Jumper or cardigan, wool — life expectancy **4 years**.
2. **Age.** Purchased 14 months before the incident. The applicable age band is **13 to 25 months**.
3. **Condition at intake.** The intake record shows no pilling, no thinning at the elbows, no previous repairs. Condition **excellent**.
4. **Table II.** The intersection of that band and that condition gives **70%**.
5. **Adjustment.** 70% × $640 = **$448.00**.
6. **The cleaning charge.** The $24.00 charged for the clean is **waived**, and the waiver is stated in the letter. We do not charge for work that produced this outcome, and the waiver is not part of the settlement figure — it is in addition to it.
7. **The offer.** $448.00, plus the waived charge.

The customer will observe that $448 does not buy the jumper again. That is correct and it is what depreciated value means, and the answer is not to apologise for the Guide but to show the working:

> *"The jumper was fourteen months into an expected four-year life, and it was in excellent condition, which is why the adjustment is seventy per cent rather than something lower. Settling at replacement cost would put you in a better position than you were in the day before you brought it to us, and that isn't how textile claims are settled anywhere in the trade."*

### 8.5 The 50% cap on a post-wedding gown

A wedding gown cleaned **after** the wedding is capped at **50% of its replacement cost**, whatever Table II otherwise produces. The Guide takes the position that the gown has served the purpose for which it was bought.

Worked through: a gown with a replacement cost of $3,200, ten months old, in excellent condition, would ordinarily attract 70% — $2,240. The cap applies, and 50% of $3,200 is **$1,600.00**. The settlement is $1,600.00.

Explain the cap explicitly and never let a customer discover it in the arithmetic. It is the single most upsetting number in this procedure and it needs its own sentence:

> *"There is one more thing I need to explain, because it will look like a deduction and it isn't. The Guide caps a gown cleaned after the wedding at half its replacement cost, on the basis that it has already done what it was bought for. So the seventy per cent becomes the cap, and the figure is $1,600."*

A gown cleaned **before** the wedding is not capped.

### 8.6 The cleaning charge

**The cleaning charge is always waived when we settle.** Every time, without being asked, and it is stated in the letter in a sentence of its own. It is a small amount of money and it does an enormous amount of work: it says we are not charging for a job that went wrong.

The waived charge is not deducted from the adjusted value and is not counted as part of the settlement. If the customer has already paid, it is refunded.

### 8.7 What happens to the garment

On payment of the full adjusted value, **the garment becomes our property**. That is the standard position under the Guide: we have paid its value, so we own it.

In practice we always offer the alternative, and we offer it in the letter rather than waiting to be asked:

> *"On payment the gown becomes ours, which is the usual position — but if you would rather keep it, say so and it's yours. Plenty of people would rather have the garment."*

Where a customer keeps the garment, the settlement is adjusted by agreement to reflect its residual value, and the agreed figure is recorded. Where we take the garment, it is retained for the life of the claim file and not disposed of, worn or sold.

## 9. The four outcomes in practice

### 9.1 Defend

**When.** Not our fault, and there is a manufacturer, retailer or supplier whose problem it properly is. Typically a component or trim failure, a fusible that has delaminated, a coating that has crazed, a dye that was never properly fixed, or a care label that does not account for the garment as made.

**Who signs it off.** Karen. Always, because it goes out in writing.

**What goes out.** A "to whom it may concern" letter addressed to nobody in particular and handed to the customer to take back to the retailer. It confirms the garment was professionally cleaned at our premises, quotes the care label exactly, states the solvent and programme actually used and the precautions applied, explains why the method was gentler than the label permitted where it was, describes the damage in textile language, names the failure mode, cites the relevant DLI TABS bulletin by title, and makes the AS/NZS 1957 point about the label where it applies.

**Tone.** Technical, not apologetic. No admission of liability, no offer of payment. It is not a letter to the customer; it is a letter *for* the customer.

**What is recorded.** The assessment, the letter, and the outcome, against the docket and in the claims register.
